front:
Complete the table of relative properties of **subatomic particles**.

| Particle | Relative charge | Relative mass |
|---|---|---|
| Proton | **..........** | **..........** |
| Neutron | **..........** | **..........** |
| Electron | **..........** | **..........** |
back:
| Particle | Relative charge | Relative mass |
|---|---|---|
| Proton | **+1** | **1** |
| Neutron | **0** | **1** |
| Electron | **-1** | **1/1836 (negligible)** |

front: Why does a beam of **electrons** deflect more than a beam of **protons** in the same electric field?
back: **Electrons** deflect more because their **mass** (~1/1836 that of a proton) is far smaller. The same electrostatic force produces a much greater acceleration on the lighter electron, causing stronger deflection.

front:
**True or False?**

In a neutral atom, the **number of electrons** equals the **number of protons**.
back:
**True.**

A neutral atom carries no overall charge, so the negatively charged **electrons** must exactly balance the positively charged **protons** in the **nucleus**.

front: Define **nucleon**.
back: A **nucleon** is a particle found in the **nucleus** of an atom. Both **protons** and **neutrons** are nucleons.

front: What happens to a beam of **neutrons** passing through an electric field?
back: A beam of **neutrons** passes straight through **without deflection**. Neutrons carry no charge and are therefore unaffected by the electric field.

front: In an atom, the **..........**  contains **protons** and **neutrons**, while **..........**  orbit in **shells** at increasing distances from the nucleus.
back: In an atom, the **nucleus** contains **protons** and **neutrons**, while **electrons** orbit in **shells** at increasing distances from the nucleus.

front: Why does the **nucleus** carry an overall **positive charge**?
back: The **nucleus** contains **protons** (relative charge +1) and **neutrons** (no charge). The positive charges of the protons are unopposed within the nucleus, giving it an overall **positive charge**.

front:
**True or False?**

The **mass** of an atom is concentrated in the **nucleus**.
back:
**True.**

**Protons** and **neutrons** each have a relative mass of 1, while the **electron** mass (~1/1836) is negligible. Almost all the mass of an atom is therefore found in the **nucleus**.

front: Define **atom**.
back: An **atom** is the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a **chemical reaction**. It consists of a central **nucleus** containing **protons** and **neutrons**, surrounded by **electrons** in **shells**.

front: In which direction is a beam of **protons** deflected in an electric field?
back: A beam of **protons** is deflected slightly toward the **negative plate**. Protons carry a positive charge and are attracted to the negative plate, but deflect less than electrons due to their much greater **mass**.

front: Define **atomic number**.
back: An **atomic number** (*Z*) is the number of **protons** in the nucleus of an atom. It is unique to each element and determines the element's identity.
Number of **neutrons** = **mass number (*****A*****)** − **atomic number (*****Z*****)**.

front: Define **mass number**.
back: A **mass number** (*A*) is the total number of **protons** and **neutrons** in the nucleus of an atom. It is also called the **nucleon number**.

front: A **Cl**<sup>**-**</sup> ion has atomic number 17 and mass number 35. How many **protons**, **neutrons**, and **electrons** does it have?
back:
A **Cl**<sup>**-**</sup> ion has:

1. **Protons:** 17 (= atomic number)
2. **Neutrons:** 18 (= 35 − 17)
3. **Electrons:** 18 (= 17 + 1, because Cl<sup>-</sup> has gained 1 electron)

front:
**True or False?**

A **Mg**<sup>**2+**</sup> ion (atomic number 12) has 12 **electrons**.
back:
**False.**

A **Mg**<sup>**2+**</sup> ion has **10 electrons**. Magnesium has atomic number 12, but the 2+ charge means it has **lost 2 electrons**, leaving 10.

front: Why does a **positive ion** have a positive charge?
back: A **positive ion** forms when an atom **loses** one or more electrons. This leaves more **protons** than electrons, so the particle has more positive charge than negative charge, giving it an overall **positive charge**.

front:
**True or False?**

All **ions** of the same element have the same number of **protons**.
back:
**True.**

The number of **protons** (the **atomic number**) is fixed for a given element and does not change when electrons are gained or lost. Only the number of **electrons** changes when ions form.

front: An unknown atom **X** has mass number 63 and 34 neutrons. How many **protons** does it have, and what element is it?
back: Atom **X** has **29 protons** (= 63 − 34). An element with atomic number 29 is **copper** (Cu).

front: **Positive** ions form when atoms **..........**  electrons, giving them **..........**  electrons than protons. **Negative** ions form when atoms **..........**  electrons.
back: **Positive** ions form when atoms **lose** electrons, giving them **fewer** electrons than protons. **Negative** ions form when atoms **gain** electrons.

front: Define **atomic radius**.
back: An **atomic radius** is a measure of the size of an atom. It is defined as half the distance between the **nuclei** of two covalently bonded atoms of the **same element**.

front: Why does **atomic radius decrease** across a period?
back: Across a period, **nuclear charge** increases as more protons are added, but electrons are added to the **same principal quantum shell**. The stronger nuclear pull draws electrons closer to the nucleus, decreasing the **atomic radius**.

front:
**True or False?**

Atomic **radius** increases across a period as more electrons are added to the outer **shell**.
back:
**False.**

Atomic **radius decreases** across a period. Although electrons are added to the same shell, the increasing **nuclear charge** pulls electrons closer to the nucleus, reducing the radius.

front: Why does **atomic radius increase** down a group?
back: Moving down a group, each element has an additional **principal quantum shell**. Electrons in inner shells **shield** outer electrons from the nuclear charge, weakening the attraction and increasing the **atomic radius**.

front: Ionic radius **..........**  with increasing negative charge, and **..........**  with increasing positive charge.
back: Ionic radius **increases** with increasing negative charge, and **decreases** with increasing positive charge.

front: Why is a **negative ion** larger than its parent atom?
back: A **negative ion** forms by gaining extra electrons while the **nuclear charge** stays the same. The greater number of electrons experience a weaker pull from the nucleus, so the **ionic radius** increases.

front:
**True or False?**

A **Ca**<sup>**2+**</sup> ion is smaller than a neutral **Ca** atom.
back:
**True.**

A **Ca**<sup>**2+**</sup> ion has lost 2 electrons while the **nuclear charge** stays the same. Fewer electrons experience a stronger pull, reducing the **ionic radius** compared to the neutral calcium atom.

front: Why does **atomic radius** increase sharply between a **noble gas** and the **alkali metal** that starts the next period?
back: The **alkali metal** at the start of the next period has one extra **principal quantum shell** compared to the noble gas. This additional shell greatly increases **shielding** and distance from the nucleus, causing a sharp rise in **atomic radius**.

front: Atomic radius generally **..........**  across a period and **..........**  down a group.
back: Atomic radius generally **decreases** across a period and **increases** down a group.

front: Define **isotopes**.
back: **Isotopes** are atoms of the same element that have the same number of **protons** and electrons, but a different number of **neutrons**. They have the same **atomic number** but different **mass numbers**.

front:
**True or False?**

Isotopes of the same element have the same **mass number**.
back:
**False.**

Isotopes of the same element have the same **atomic number** (same number of protons) but **different mass numbers** because they contain different numbers of **neutrons**.

front: How are **isotopes** named?
back: Isotopes are named using the **chemical symbol** (or element name) followed by a dash and the **mass number**. For example, carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon with 6 and 8 neutrons respectively.

front: Isotopes of the same element have the same **..........**  properties but different **..........**  properties.
back: Isotopes of the same element have the same **chemical** properties but different **physical** properties.

front: Why do **isotopes** of the same element have identical **chemical** properties?
back: Isotopes have the same number of **electrons** and the same **electron configuration**. Because chemical behaviour is determined by **electrons** (especially those in the outer shell), all isotopes of an element react in the same way.

front:
**True or False?**

Isotopes of the same element have the same **density**.
back:
**False.**

Isotopes have different numbers of **neutrons**, so they have different **masses**. This leads to differences in **density** and **relative atomic mass**, even though their chemical properties are identical.

front: Why do **isotopes** of the same element differ in **physical** properties?
back: Isotopes differ in the number of **neutrons**, which changes the nuclear **mass** without affecting charge. This leads to different **relative atomic masses**, **densities** and behaviour in processes such as **mass spectrometry**.

front: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are isotopes of chlorine. They have the same **..........**  of 17 but different **..........**  (35 and 37).
back: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are isotopes of chlorine. They have the same **atomic number** of 17 but different **mass numbers** (35 and 37).

front: Carbon-14 has an atomic number of 6 and mass number 14. How many **protons**, **neutrons** and **electrons** does a neutral carbon-14 atom have?
back:
A neutral **carbon-14** atom has:

1. **Protons:** 6 (= atomic number)
2. **Neutrons:** 8 (= 14 − 6)
3. **Electrons:** 6 (neutral atom, so electrons = protons)

front: Define **electronic configuration**.
back: An **electronic configuration** is the arrangement of **electrons** in the **shells** and **subshells** of an atom. In the ground state, electrons fill from the lowest energy shell upward.

front: Shell *n* = 3 can hold a maximum of **..........**  electrons, and shell *n* = 4 can hold a maximum of **..........**  electrons.
back: Shell *n* = 3 can hold a maximum of **18** electrons, and shell *n* = 4 can hold a maximum of **32** electrons.

front:
**True or False?**

The *n* = 3 principal quantum **shell** can hold a maximum of 8 **electrons**.
back:
**False.**

The *n* = 3 shell can hold a maximum of **18 electrons**. The capacity increases with shell number: *n* = 1 holds 2, *n* = 2 holds 8, *n* = 3 holds 18 and *n* = 4 holds 32.

front: Why is the **4s orbital** filled before the **3d orbital**?
back: The **4s orbital** has slightly lower **energy** than the **3d orbital**, despite being in a higher principal quantum shell. Electrons always fill the **lowest energy** orbital first, so 4s fills before 3d.

front: Define **orbital**.
back: An **orbital** is a region of space around the **nucleus** where there is a high probability of finding an **electron**. Each orbital can hold a maximum of **2 electrons**.

front:
**True or False?**

A higher **principal quantum number** corresponds to a higher energy **shell**.
back:
**True.**

As the **principal quantum number** (*n*) increases, the shell is further from the nucleus and has higher **energy**. Electrons in outer shells are held less tightly than those in inner shells.

front: What is the **ground state** of an atom?
back: The **ground state** is the most stable electronic configuration of an atom, in which electrons occupy the **lowest available energy** subshells first (starting with 1s).

front: In order of increasing energy, the subshells are: s, **..........**,  **..........**  and **..........**.
back: In order of increasing energy, the subshells are: s, **p**, **d** and **f**.

front: How many **electrons** can the *n* = 2 shell hold, and why?
back: The *n* = 2 shell can hold **8 electrons**. It contains one **s** subshell (2 electrons) and one **p** subshell (6 electrons), giving a total of 2 + 6 = **8 electrons**.

front: Define **degenerate** orbitals.
back: **Degenerate** orbitals are orbitals within the same **subshell** that have identical **energies**. For example, the three **p** orbitals (p<sub>x</sub>, p<sub>y</sub> and p<sub>z</sub>) within a given shell are all degenerate.

front: The **p** subshell holds a maximum of **..........**  electrons and the **d** subshell holds a maximum of **..........**  electrons.
back: The **p** subshell holds a maximum of **6** electrons and the **d** subshell holds a maximum of **10** electrons.

front: How many **orbitals** does the **p** subshell contain, and what are they called?
back: The **p** subshell contains **3 orbitals**, labelled p<sub>x</sub>, p<sub>y</sub> and p<sub>z</sub>. Each orbital holds up to 2 electrons, so the p subshell holds a maximum of **6 electrons** in total.

front:
**True or False?**

The **p** orbitals are **spherical** in shape.
back:
**False.**

The **p** orbitals are **dumbbell-shaped**, with two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus. It is the **s** orbital that is spherical.

front: Describe the shape and size trend of **s** orbitals.
back: The **s** orbital is **spherical** in shape. Its size increases with the **principal quantum number**. The 3s orbital is larger than the 2s, which is larger than the 1s.

front:
**True or False?**

All orbitals within the same **subshell** have the same **energy**.
back:
**True.**

Orbitals within the same subshell are **degenerate**, meaning they have identical energies. For example, p<sub>x</sub>, p<sub>y</sub> and p<sub>z</sub> all have the same energy within a given **p** subshell.

front: How are the three **p** orbitals arranged relative to one another?
back: The three **p** orbitals (p<sub>x</sub>, p<sub>y</sub> and p<sub>z</sub>) are oriented along the **x**, **y** and **z** axes. They point **perpendicular** to one another, so the lobes of each orbital are at right angles to the other two.

front: The **s** subshell contains **..........**  orbital, the **p** subshell contains **..........**  orbitals and the **d** subshell contains **..........**  orbitals.
back: The **s** subshell contains **1** orbital, the **p** subshell contains **3** orbitals and the **d** subshell contains **5** orbitals.

front: How many **electrons** can the **f** subshell hold, and why?
back: The **f** subshell can hold **14 electrons**. It contains **7 orbitals**, and each orbital holds a maximum of **2 electrons** (7 × 2 = 14).

front: Define **electron box notation**.
back: An **electron box notation** is a diagram showing electrons as arrows within boxes, each box representing one orbital, used to display electron spin and filling order.

front: Electrons occupy the **..........**-energy orbitals available first. Within a sub-shell, electrons fill **..........**  orbitals before pairing.
back: Electrons occupy the **lowest**-energy orbitals available first. Within a sub-shell, electrons fill **separate** orbitals before pairing.

front: Why do two electrons in the same orbital have opposite spins?
back: Opposite spins minimise electron repulsion (spin-pair repulsion), making this the lower-energy arrangement.

front:
**True or False?**

Three electrons can occupy the same orbital.
back:
**False.**

Each orbital holds a maximum of two electrons, which must have opposite spins.

front: Why do electrons in the same sub-shell occupy separate orbitals before pairing?
back: Occupying separate orbitals reduces electron-electron repulsion, giving a lower overall energy.

front: Define **free radical**.
back: A **free radical** is a species with one or more unpaired electrons.

front:
**True or False?**

Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins.
back:
**True.**

Opposite spins reduce spin-pair repulsion and are required by the Pauli exclusion principle.

front: Write the full electron configuration of carbon (Z = 6).
back: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>2</sup>

front: Hund's rule states that electrons in the same sub-shell occupy **..........**  orbitals with the **..........** spin before pairing up.
back: Hund's rule states that electrons in the same sub-shell occupy **separate** orbitals with the **same** spin before pairing up.

front: Define **shorthand electron configuration**.
back: A **shorthand electron configuration** is a way of writing electron arrangement using the symbol of the previous noble gas in square brackets to represent inner electrons, followed by the remaining sub-shells. For example, potassium: [Ar] 4s<sup>1</sup>.

front: Transition metals fill the **..........** sub-shell before **..........**, but lose electrons from **..........** first when forming ions.
back: Transition metals fill the **4s** sub-shell before **3d**, but lose electrons from **4s** first when forming ions.

front: What is the shorthand electron configuration of chromium (Cr, Z = 24)?
back: [Ar] 3d<sup>5</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup>. The expected [Ar] 3d<sup>4</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup> is not observed because a half-filled 3d sub-shell is energetically favourable, so one electron is promoted from 4s.

front:
**True or False?**

Copper has the electron configuration [Ar] 3d<sup>9</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup>.
back:
**False.**

Copper's configuration is [Ar] 3d<sup>10</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup>. A fully filled 3d sub-shell is energetically favourable, so one electron is promoted from 4s.

front: Write the shorthand electron configuration of Fe<sup>2+</sup> (Z = 26).
back: Iron has the configuration [Ar] 4s<sup>2</sup> 3d<sup>6</sup>. Fe<sup>2+</sup> loses two electrons from 4s first, giving [Ar] 3d<sup>6</sup>.

front: In the periodic table, elements with valence electrons in an s orbital belong to the **..........** block, in a p orbital to the **..........** block, and in a d orbital to the **..........** block.
back: In the periodic table, elements with valence electrons in an s orbital belong to the **s** block, in a p orbital to the **p** block, and in a d orbital to the **d** block.

front: Write the shorthand electron configuration of gallium (Ga, Z = 31).
back: [Ar] 3d<sup>10</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup> 4p<sup>1</sup>

front:
**True or False?**

When filling electron configurations, the 3d sub-shell is filled before the 4s sub-shell.
back:
**False.**

The 4s sub-shell has lower energy than 3d and fills first. However, when forming ions, electrons are lost from 4s before 3d.

front: Write the shorthand electron configuration of Ca<sup>2+</sup> (Z = 20).
back: Calcium is [Ar] 4s<sup>2</sup>. Ca<sup>2+</sup> loses both 4s electrons, giving the same configuration as argon: [Ar].

front: Define **ionisation energy**.
back: An **ionisation energy** (**IE**) is the energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms of an element, forming one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.

front: Ionisation energies are measured under standard conditions of **..........**  K and **..........** kPa, and have units of **..........** .
back: Ionisation energies are measured under standard conditions of **298** K and **101** kPa, and have units of **kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>.

front: Why are ionisation energies always positive values?
back: **Ionisation** is endothermic, so energy must be supplied to overcome the force of attraction between the electron and the positive nucleus.

front:
**True or False?**

The first ionisation energy involves removing an electron from a gaseous 1+ ion.
back:
**False.**

The first IE involves removing an electron from a neutral gaseous atom, producing a gaseous 1+ ion. The second IE involves removal from a gaseous 1+ ion.

front: Write the equation for the first ionisation energy of calcium.
back: Ca (g) → Ca<sup>+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup>          IE<sub>1</sub> = +590 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

front: The second ionisation energy is the energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous **..........** ions to form one mole of gaseous **..........** ions.
back: The second ionisation energy is the energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous **1+** ions to form one mole of gaseous **2+** ions.

front: Write the equation for the second ionisation energy of calcium.
back: Ca<sup>+</sup> (g) → Ca<sup>2+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup>          IE<sub>2</sub> = +1145.4 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

front:
**True or False?**

The equation Ca (g) → Ca<sup>2+</sup> (g) + 2e<sup>-</sup> correctly represents an ionisation energy.
back:
**False.**

Ionisation energies must be written one step at a time, removing one mole of electrons per equation. This equation represents two separate ionisation steps combined.

front: Why must atoms in ionisation energy equations be in the gaseous state?
back: Ionisation energy is defined specifically for gaseous species. Including solid or liquid atoms would incorporate the energy of vaporisation, which is not part of the IE definition.

front: Define **electron shielding**.
back: An **electron shielding** is the reduction in effective nuclear charge experienced by outer electrons, caused by repulsion from inner-shell electrons that partially block the attraction of the nucleus.

front: Across a period, first ionisation energy generally **..........**  because nuclear charge **..........**  while shielding remains roughly **..........** and atomic radius **..........**.
back: Across a period, first ionisation energy generally **increases** because nuclear charge **increases** while shielding remains roughly **constant** and atomic radius **decreases**.

front: Explain why first ionisation energy decreases down a group.
back: Down a group, atomic radius increases and shielding increases as more electron shells are added. Both effects weaken the attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons, outweighing the increased nuclear charge.

front:
**True or False?**

Successive ionisation energies for a given element always increase.
back:
**True.**

Removing each electron leaves an increasingly positive ion, so the remaining electrons are held more tightly by the nucleus and require more energy to remove.

front: Why is the first ionisation energy of oxygen lower than that of nitrogen?
back: Oxygen has two electrons paired in the 2p<sup>x</sup> orbital. Spin-pair repulsion makes it easier to remove one of these paired electrons, lowering the first IE relative to nitrogen, where each 2p orbital holds only one electron.

front: A large jump in successive ionisation energies indicates an electron is being removed from a new **..........**  closer to the nucleus. The number of electrons removed **before** the jump equals the number of **..........** electrons.
back: A large jump in successive ionisation energies indicates an electron is being removed from a new **inner shell** closer to the nucleus. The number of electrons removed **before** the jump equals the number of **valence** electrons.

front: Why is the first ionisation energy of boron lower than that of beryllium?
back: Boron's outer electron is in the 2p sub-shell, which is at a higher energy level and further from the nucleus than beryllium's 2s outer electrons, so less energy is needed to remove it.

front:
**True or False?**

A large jump between the first and second ionisation energies of an element indicates it belongs to Group 1.
back:
**True.**

Only one valence electron is removed before the large jump, indicating the element has one outer-shell electron, a defining feature of Group 1 elements.

front: State four factors that affect ionisation energy.
back:
1. Nuclear charge: higher charge increases IE.
2. Distance from the nucleus: greater distance decreases IE.
3. Electron shielding: more inner shells decrease IE.
4. Spin-pair repulsion: paired electrons in an orbital decrease IE.

front: Define **successive ionisation energies**.
back: **Successive ionisation energies** are the energies required to remove each subsequent mole of electrons from one mole of a gaseous element, one electron at a time from an increasingly positive ion.

front: How can successive ionisation energy data be used to determine an element's group?
back: Identify the largest jump between consecutive ionisation energies. The number of electrons removed before that jump equals the number of valence electrons, which gives the group number for s- and p-block elements.

front: As successive electrons are removed, ionisation energies increase because the ion becomes more **..........**  , increasing the attraction between the nucleus and the **..........** electrons.
back: As successive electrons are removed, ionisation energies increase because the ion becomes more **positive**, increasing the attraction between the nucleus and the **remaining** electrons.

front:
**True or False?**

If the largest jump in successive ionisation energy data occurs between the 3rd and 4th IE, the element has 3 valence electrons.
back:
**True.**

The jump occurs because the 4th electron is removed from a new inner shell. The 3 electrons removed before the jump are the valence electrons.

front: Identify the Period 3 element with a large jump between IE<sub>7</sub> and IE<sub>8</sub>.
back: Seven electrons are removed before the large jump, indicating 7 valence electrons and Group 17. The Period 3 element in Group 17 is chlorine (Cl), with configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>5</sup>.

front: To deduce electronic configuration from successive IE data, locate the **..........** increase between consecutive IEs. Electrons removed **before** this jump represent the **..........** electrons.
back: To deduce electronic configuration from successive IE data, locate the **largest** increase between consecutive IEs. Electrons removed **before** this jump represent the **valence** electrons.

front: Why does a large jump occur in successive ionisation energies?
back: The large jump occurs when an electron is removed from a new inner shell closer to the nucleus. These electrons experience less shielding and stronger nuclear attraction, so much more energy is required to remove them.

front:
**True or False?**

The position of the large jump in successive ionisation energy data indicates an element's period.
back:
**False.**

The position of the large jump indicates the number of valence electrons and therefore the element's group, not its period.

front: Explain why a large jump between IE<sub>2</sub> and IE<sub>3</sub> suggests an element is in Group 2.
back: Two electrons are removed before the large jump, indicating 2 valence electrons. For s- and p-block elements, the number of valence electrons equals the group number, so the element belongs to Group 2.

front: Define **unified atomic mass unit**.
back: A **unified atomic mass unit** is defined as one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. Its symbol is *u* (or Da, Dalton), and 1 *u* = 1.66 x 10<sup>-27</sup> kg.

front: How is the relative atomic mass (*A*<sub>r</sub>) of an element calculated from its isotopes?
back: Multiply each isotope's **mass number** by its **percentage abundance**, sum the results, then divide by 100. This gives the weighted average of the isotope masses.

front:
**True or False?**

Relative atomic mass has units of grams.
back:
**False.**

Relative atomic mass is a ratio (mass of one atom relative to one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom), so the units cancel and it is dimensionless.

front: The relative atomic mass (*A*<sub>r</sub>) is the ratio of the average mass of atoms of an element to the **..........**, defined as one-twelfth of the mass of a **..........**  atom.
back: The relative atomic mass (*A*<sub>r</sub>) is the ratio of the average mass of atoms of an element to the **unified atomic mass unit**, defined as one-twelfth of the mass of a **carbon-12** atom.

front: Define **relative isotopic mass**.
back: **Relative isotopic mass** is the mass of one atom of a specific isotope compared to the value of the unified atomic mass unit.

front: What is the relative molecular mass (*M*<sub>r</sub>) of water (H<sub>2</sub>O)? (A<sub>r</sub>: H = 1.0, O = 16.0)
back: *M*<sub>r</sub> = (2 x 1.0) + (1 x 16.0) = **18.0**. It is calculated by summing the relative atomic masses of all atoms in one molecule.

front:
**True or False?**

Isotopes of an element have the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons.
back:
**False.**

Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, giving them different mass numbers.

front: The relative **..........**  mass (*M*<sub>r</sub>) is used for ionic compounds. It is calculated in the same way as the relative **..........**  mass by summing the relative atomic masses of all atoms in the formula unit.
back: The relative **formula** mass (*M*<sub>r</sub>) is used for ionic compounds. It is calculated in the same way as the relative **molecular** mass by summing the relative atomic masses of all atoms in the formula unit.

front: Define **relative molecular mass**.
back: **Relative molecular mass** (*M*<sub>r</sub>) is the ratio of the weighted average mass of a molecule of a molecular compound to the unified atomic mass unit. It has no units and is found by adding the relative atomic masses of all atoms in one molecule.

front: Define **the Avogadro constant**.
back: The **Avogadro constant** (*N*<sub>A</sub>) is 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>. It is the number of particles (atoms, molecules, ions or electrons) in one mole of a substance.

front:
**True or False?**

One mole of any element has a mass equal to its relative atomic mass in grams.
back:
**True.**

For example, one mole of sodium (A<sub>r</sub> = 23.0) has a mass of 23.0 g, and one mole of carbon (A<sub>r</sub> = 12.0) has a mass of 12.0 g.

front: How many molecules are in 1 mole of H<sub>2</sub>, and how many individual H atoms does this correspond to?
back: 1 mole of H<sub>2</sub> contains **6.02 × 10**<sup>**23**</sup> molecules. Since each molecule has 2 H atoms, this corresponds to 2 × 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> = **1.204 × 10**<sup>**24**</sup> H atoms.

front: The Avogadro constant is **..........**  mol<sup>-1</sup>. A substance containing this many particles has a mass called one **..........** .
back: The Avogadro constant is **6.02 x 10**<sup>**23**</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>. A substance containing this many particles has a mass called one **mole**.

front: Define **mole**.
back: A **mole** is the amount of substance that contains the same number of fundamental units as there are atoms in exactly 12.00 g of carbon-12. This number is 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup>.

front: What is the mass of 1 mole of NaCl? (A<sub>r</sub>: Na = 23.0, Cl = 35.5)
back: Mass = 23.0 + 35.5 = **58.5 g mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>. The molar mass is found by summing the relative atomic masses of all atoms in the formula unit.

front:
**True or False?**

The Avogadro constant applies only to atoms and molecules, not to ions or electrons.
back:
**False.**

The Avogadro constant applies to atoms, molecules, ions and electrons.

front: One mole of water (H<sub>2</sub>O) has a mass of **..........**  g, because the relative atomic masses of hydrogen and oxygen are **..........**  and **..........**  respectively.
back: One mole of water (H<sub>2</sub>O) has a mass of **18** g, because the relative atomic masses of hydrogen and oxygen are **1.0** and **16.0** respectively.

front: How many total atoms are in 1 mole of NaCl?
back: 1 mole of NaCl contains **1.204 × 10**<sup>**24**</sup> atoms in total, because each formula unit has one Na atom and one Cl atom, giving 2 × 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> atoms.

front: Define **compound ion**.
back: A **compound ion** is an ion that contains more than one type of element, such as hydroxide (OH<sup>-</sup>), sulfate (SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>) or nitrate (NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>).

front: What is the formula of magnesium chloride? Explain how you determine it.
back: The formula is **MgCl**<sub>**2**</sub>. Magnesium (Group 2) has a 2+ charge and chlorine (Group 17) has a 1- charge. Two Cl<sup>-</sup> ions are needed to balance one Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion.

front:
**True or False?**

Ionic compounds are electrically neutral because the total positive charge equals the total negative charge.
back:
**True.**

In any ionic compound, the charges from positive and negative ions must balance exactly, giving an overall charge of zero.

front: Elements in Group 17 gain **..........**  electron(s) to form ions with a **..........**  charge, while elements in Group 16 gain **..........**  electrons to form ions with a 2- charge.
back: Elements in Group 17 gain **1** electron(s) to form ions with a **1-** charge, while elements in Group 16 gain **2** electrons to form ions with a 2- charge.

front: What is the formula of iron(III) oxide? Explain how you determine it.
back: The formula is **Fe**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**<sub>**3**</sub>. Iron(III) has a 3+ charge and oxygen (Group 16) has a 2- charge. Two Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions (6+) balance three O<sup>2-</sup> ions (6-).

front: Define **Roman numerals in compound names**.
back: **Roman numerals in compound names** are symbols used to indicate the charge (oxidation state) of the metal ion. They are used for transition metals whose charges can vary. For example, copper(II) has a 2+ charge.

front:
**True or False?**

Ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) is an example of a non-metal positive ion.
back:
**True.**

Most positive ions are metals, but ammonium (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) and hydrogen (H<sup>+</sup>) are non-metal positive ions.

front: The formula of aluminium nitrate is **..........**  because aluminium has a **..........**  charge and nitrate (NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>) has a 1- charge.
back: The formula of aluminium nitrate is **Al(NO**<sub>**3**</sub>**)**<sub>**3**</sub> because aluminium has a **3+** charge and nitrate (NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>) has a 1- charge.

front: What charges do Group 1, Group 2 and Group 13 metals form when they become ions?
back: **Group 1** metals form **1+** ions, **Group 2** metals form **2+** ions and **Group 13** metals form **3+** ions.

front: Define **spectator ions**.
back: **Spectator ions** are ions present in solution that do not take part in a chemical reaction. They appear on both sides of the full ionic equation and are cancelled out when writing the net ionic equation.

front: What are the four state symbols used in chemical equations and what do they represent?
back: (s) = **solid**, (l) = **liquid**, (g) = **gas**, (aq) = **aqueous** (dissolved in water).

front:
**True or False?**

When balancing an equation, you can change the formulae of reactants or products to make the numbers work.
back:
**False.**

You must never change the formulae. Only the coefficients (numbers placed in front of formulae) may be changed when balancing an equation.

front: The balanced equation for magnesium burning in oxygen is **..........**  Mg (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → **..........**  MgO (s).
back: The balanced equation for magnesium burning in oxygen is **2** Mg (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → **2** MgO (s).

front: Define **ionic equation**.
back: An **ionic equation** is a chemical equation showing only the ions and particles that actually take part in a reaction. Spectator ions are omitted and are cancelled from both sides of the full ionic equation.

front: Write the net ionic equation for the reaction of zinc with copper(II) sulfate solution.
back: Zn (s) + Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) → Zn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + Cu (s). The sulfate ion (SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>) is a spectator ion and is cancelled from both sides.

front:
**True or False?**

In a balanced chemical equation, atoms can be created or destroyed as long as the overall mass is conserved.
back:
**False.**

Atoms cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction. The number of each type of atom must be identical on both sides of the equation.

front: When balancing combustion reactions of organic compounds, balance the **..........**  atoms first, then **..........**  and finally **..........** .
back: When balancing combustion reactions of organic compounds, balance the **carbon** atoms first, then **hydrogen** and finally **oxygen**.

front: What is the difference between a word equation and a symbol equation?
back: A **word equation** uses only words to show reactants and products. A **symbol equation** uses chemical symbols and formulae to show the number and type of each atom involved in the reaction.

front: Define **empirical formula**.
back: An **empirical formula** is the simplest whole-number ratio of the elements present in one molecule or formula unit of a compound. For example, the empirical formula of ethanoic acid (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) is CH<sub>2</sub>O.

front: How do you calculate the empirical formula from the masses of elements present in a compound?
back: Divide the mass of each element by its **relative atomic mass** to find **moles**. Then divide all values by the smallest to get the **simplest whole-number ratio**.

front:
**True or False?**

Ionic compounds always have the same empirical and molecular formulae.
back:
**True.**

Ionic compounds are represented by their simplest formula unit, so their empirical and molecular formulae are always the same.

front: To find the molecular formula from the empirical formula, divide the **..........**  of the molecular formula by the **..........**  of the empirical formula, then multiply each subscript by this number.
back: To find the molecular formula from the empirical formula, divide the **relative formula mass** of the molecular formula by the **relative formula mass** of the empirical formula, then multiply each subscript by this number.

front: Define **molecular formula**.
back: A **molecular formula** is the exact number of atoms of each element present in one molecule of a compound. For example, ethanoic acid has the molecular formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

front: A compound contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass. What is its empirical formula? (A<sub>r</sub>: C = 12.0, H = 1.0)
back: Moles of C = 85.7/12.0 = 7.14. Moles of H = 14.3/1.0 = 14.3. Ratio = 1:2. Empirical formula = **CH**<sub>**2**</sub>.

front:
**True or False?**

Organic molecules always have the same empirical and molecular formulae.
back:
**False.**

Organic molecules often have different empirical and molecular formulae. For example, ethanoic acid has empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub>O and molecular formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

front: A compound contains 10 g of hydrogen and 80 g of oxygen. The mole ratio of H to O is **..........**  to **..........**  giving the empirical formula **..........** .
back: A compound contains 10 g of hydrogen and 80 g of oxygen. The mole ratio of H to O is **2** to **1** giving the empirical formula **H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**.

front: The empirical formula of compound X is C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>S and its relative formula mass is 180. What is the molecular formula of X? (A<sub>r</sub>: C = 12, H = 1, S = 32)
back: M<sub>r</sub> of empirical formula = (4x12) + (10x1) + 32 = 90. Ratio = 180/90 = 2. Molecular formula = **C**<sub>**8**</sub>**H**<sub>**20**</sub>**S**<sub>**2**</sub>.

front: Define **water of crystallisation**.
back: **Water of crystallisation** is water that is chemically incorporated into the crystal structure of a compound. It is shown in the formula by a dot, e.g. CuSO<sub>4</sub>•5H<sub>2</sub>O.

front:
**True or False?**

A hydrated compound contains water of crystallisation as part of its structure.
back:
**True.**

A hydrated compound incorporates water molecules into its crystal lattice. An anhydrous compound contains no water of crystallisation.

front: How can you convert a hydrated salt to its anhydrous form, and how is this reversed?
back: **Heating** the hydrated salt drives off the **water of crystallisation** to give the **anhydrous** compound. Adding water reverses the process, reforming the hydrated salt.

front: The formula of hydrated copper(II) sulfate is **..........**  and the formula of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is **..........** .
back: The formula of hydrated copper(II) sulfate is **CuSO**<sub>**4**</sub>**•5H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O** and the formula of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is **CuSO**<sub>**4**</sub>.

front: Define **anhydrous compound**.
back: An **anhydrous compound** is a compound that contains no water of crystallisation. It is the form obtained when a hydrated salt is fully dried by heating.

front: Describe the experimental steps used to determine the degree of hydration (water of crystallisation) of a hydrated salt.
back: Measure the mass of the **hydrated salt** before heating. Heat until **constant mass** is achieved. Calculate the mass of water lost, then use **mole ratios** (dividing by respective M<sub>r</sub> values) to find the number of water molecules.

front:
**True or False?**

A compound can only be hydrated to one fixed degree.
back:
**False.**

A compound can be hydrated to different degrees. For example, cobalt(II) chloride can form CoCl<sub>2</sub>•6H<sub>2</sub>O or CoCl<sub>2</sub>•2H<sub>2</sub>O.

front: 10.0 g of CuSO<sub>4</sub>•xH<sub>2</sub>O is heated to give 5.59 g of CuSO<sub>4</sub>. The mass of water lost is **..........**  g. Dividing by the M<sub>r</sub> of water (18.0) gives **..........**  mol H<sub>2</sub>O.
back: 10.0 g of CuSO<sub>4</sub>•xH<sub>2</sub>O is heated to give 5.59 g of CuSO<sub>4</sub>. The mass of water lost is **4.41** g. Dividing by the M<sub>r</sub> of water (18.0) gives **0.245** mol H<sub>2</sub>O.

front: How is a water of crystallisation calculation similar to an empirical formula calculation?
back: Both involve dividing masses by **formula masses** to find **moles**, then dividing by the smallest value to get the **simplest ratio**. In water of crystallisation calculations the salt and water replace the individual elements.

front: Define **limiting reagent**.
back: A **limiting reagent** is the reactant that is completely consumed in a reaction. It determines the maximum amount of product that can be formed and is not present in excess.

front: What is the molar volume of any gas at room temperature and pressure (RTP), and what are the RTP conditions?
back: At RTP (20 °C, 1 atm), one mole of any gas occupies **24.0 dm**<sup>**3**</sup>. This is Avogadro's hypothesis applied to gases.

front:
**True or False?**

Percentage yield compares the actual yield with the maximum theoretical yield.
back:
**True.**

Percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100. It shows how much of the expected product was actually obtained.

front: Concentration (mol dm<sup>-3</sup>) = **..........**  divided by **..........** . To convert cm<sup>3</sup> to dm<sup>3</sup>, divide by **..........** .
back: Concentration (mol dm<sup>-3</sup>) = **moles of solute** divided by **volume of solution (dm**<sup>**3**</sup>**)**. To convert cm<sup>3</sup> to dm<sup>3</sup>, divide by **1000**.

front: Define **percentage yield**.
back: **Percentage yield** is the ratio of the actual yield obtained experimentally to the predicted theoretical yield, expressed as a percentage. It is calculated as: (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100.

front: 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.050 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> is neutralised by 20.0 cm<sup>3</sup> HCl. What is the concentration of HCl? (Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub>)
back: Moles Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> = 0.025 x 0.050 = 0.00125 mol. Moles HCl = 2 x 0.00125 = 0.00250 mol. Concentration HCl = 0.00250/0.020 = **0.125 mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>.

front:
**True or False?**

Equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules.
back:
**True.**

This is Avogadro's hypothesis. It means that mole ratios from balanced equations apply directly to gas volumes at the same conditions.

front: The number of moles of a substance = **..........**  divided by **..........** . A mass of 6.0 g of Mg (M<sub>r</sub> = 24.3) gives **..........**  moles.
back: The number of moles of a substance = **mass (g)** divided by **molar mass (g mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>**)**. A mass of 6.0 g of Mg (M<sub>r</sub> = 24.3) gives **0.247** moles.

front: In a reaction of 9.2 g Na with 8.0 g S to form Na<sub>2</sub>S, which is the limiting reagent? (2Na + S → Na<sub>2</sub>S; A<sub>r</sub>: Na = 23.0, S = 32.1)
back: Moles Na = 9.2/23.0 = 0.40 mol. Moles S = 8.0/32.1 = 0.25 mol. To react 0.40 mol Na requires only 0.20 mol S. S is in excess, so **Na is the limiting reagent**.

front: Define **electronegativity**.
back: **Electronegativity** is the ability of an atom to attract a pair of electrons towards itself in a covalent bond.

front: Which scale is used to measure electronegativity, and what value does it assign to fluorine?
back: The **Pauling scale** is used. Fluorine has the highest value of **4.0**, making it the most electronegative element on the periodic table.

front:
**True or False?**

An increased nuclear charge results in a decreased electronegativity.
back:
**False.**

An increased nuclear charge means more protons attract outer electrons more strongly, so electronegativity **increases**.

front: Electronegativity **..........**  across a period and **..........**  down a group.
back: Electronegativity **increases** across a period and **decreases** down a group.

front: Define **shielding (electronegativity)**.
back: **Shielding** is the reduction in nuclear attraction experienced by outer electrons due to filled inner energy levels masking the positive charge of the nucleus.

front: How does atomic radius affect electronegativity?
back: A larger atomic radius means outer electrons are further from the nucleus and experience weaker attraction, so electronegativity **decreases** as atomic radius increases.

front:
**True or False?**

Sodium has a higher electronegativity than caesium.
back:
**True.**

Sodium has fewer inner shells than caesium, so its outer electrons experience less shielding and are more strongly attracted to the nucleus.

front: In the C-F bond of fluoromethane, the bonding electrons are drawn closer to the **..........**  atom because it has a higher **..........** .
back: In the C-F bond of fluoromethane, the bonding electrons are drawn closer to the **fluorine** atom because it has a higher **electronegativity**.

front: State the three factors that affect the electronegativity of an atom.
back:
1. **Nuclear charge** — more protons increase electronegativity.
2. **Atomic radius** — a larger radius decreases electronegativity.
3. **Shielding** — more inner shells decrease electronegativity.

front: Why does electronegativity decrease down a group in the periodic table?
back: Each successive element has an extra filled electron shell, increasing **shielding** and **atomic radius**. Although nuclear charge increases, the overall attraction between the nucleus and outer bonding electrons decreases.

front:
**True or False?**

Shielding increases significantly across a period.
back:
**False.**

Shielding remains reasonably **constant** across a period because no new electron shells are added.

front: Across a period, nuclear charge **..........**  while atomic radius **..........**  , causing electronegativity to **..........** .
back: Across a period, nuclear charge **increases** while atomic radius **decreases**, causing electronegativity to **increase**.

front: Define **trend in electronegativity across a period**.
back: The **trend in electronegativity across a period** is the general increase in electronegativity from left to right across a period, driven by increasing nuclear charge with roughly constant shielding.

front: In which direction on the periodic table is electronegativity at its highest, and which element is the most electronegative?
back: Electronegativity is greatest towards the **top right** of the periodic table. **Fluorine** is the most electronegative element.

front:
**True or False?**

Atomic radius increases across a period.
back:
**False.**

Atomic radius **decreases** across a period because nuclear charge increases while shielding stays roughly constant, pulling outer electrons closer.

front: Down a group, shielding **..........**  and atomic radius **..........**  , so electronegativity **..........** .
back: Down a group, shielding **increases** and atomic radius **increases**, so electronegativity **decreases**.

front: What happens to nuclear charge down a group, and why does electronegativity still decrease?
back: Nuclear charge **increases** down a group, but the effect is outweighed by the **increased shielding** and **larger atomic radius** caused by additional electron shells, reducing the attraction for bonding electrons.

front:
**True or False?**

Nuclear charge increases both across a period and down a group.
back:
**True.**

Nuclear charge increases in both directions as protons are added to the nucleus, but its effect on electronegativity differs because shielding and atomic radius change differently in each direction.

front: Define **polar covalent bond**.
back: A **polar covalent bond** is a covalent bond in which the bonding electrons are unequally shared due to a difference in electronegativity between the two atoms, creating partial positive (δ<sup>+</sup>) and partial negative (δ<sup>-</sup>) charges.

front: What electronegativity difference (ΔEN) range indicates a polar covalent bond?
back: A ΔEN of approximately **0.4–1.7** indicates a polar covalent bond. Below <sub>0.4 the bond is non-polar covalent; above </sub>1.7 the bond is mostly ionic.

front:
**True or False?**

In H<sub>2</sub>, the bonding electrons are shared equally between the two hydrogen atoms.
back:
**True.**

Both hydrogen atoms have the same electronegativity, so there is no difference in attraction for the bonding electrons, forming a non-polar covalent bond.

front: In hydrogen fluoride, fluorine carries a partial **..........**  charge (δ<sup>-</sup>) and hydrogen carries a partial **..........**  charge (δ<sup>+</sup>) because fluorine is more **..........** .
back: In hydrogen fluoride, fluorine carries a partial **negative** charge (δ<sup>-</sup>) and hydrogen carries a partial **positive** charge (δ<sup>+</sup>) because fluorine is more **electronegative**.

front: Define **non-polar covalent bond**.
back: A **non-polar covalent bond** is a covalent bond formed between two atoms of equal electronegativity, where the bonding electrons are shared equally and no partial charges develop.

front: How does a large difference in electronegativity between two atoms lead to ionic bond formation?
back: When ΔEN is large (greater than ~1.7), the more electronegative atom attracts electrons so strongly that the less electronegative atom's electron is **transferred** completely, forming a cation (positive) and an anion (negative) held by an ionic bond.

front:
**True or False?**

A polar bond always results in a polar molecule.
back:
**False.**

A polar molecule requires that bond dipoles do **not** cancel out. In some symmetrical molecules, polar bonds cancel, giving a non-polar molecule overall.

front: A cation is a **..........**  charged species formed when an atom **..........**  one or more electrons during ionic bond formation.
back: A cation is a **positively** charged species formed when an atom **loses** one or more electrons during ionic bond formation.

front: State the type of bond formed when ΔEN ≈ 0 and explain why.
back: A **non-polar covalent bond** forms. Both atoms have equal electronegativity so the bonding electrons are shared equally, with no partial charges developing.

front: Define **ionic bond**.
back: An **ionic bond** is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when electrons are transferred from a metal atom (forming a cation) to a non-metal atom (forming an anion).

front: What electronic configuration do ions typically adopt after ionic bond formation?
back: Ions adopt the electronic configuration of the nearest **noble gas**, giving them a full outer shell. For example, K<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> both have the configuration [2,8,8], the same as argon.

front:
**True or False?**

In ionic bonding, the metal atom gains electrons to form a cation.
back:
**False.**

The **metal atom loses** electrons to form a positively charged cation. The non-metal atom gains electrons to form a negatively charged anion.

front: Ionic compounds form a **..........**  structure in which cations and anions are arranged in a regular repeating pattern so the overall compound is electrically **..........**  .
back: Ionic compounds form a **lattice** structure in which cations and anions are arranged in a regular repeating pattern so the overall compound is electrically **neutral**.

front: Define **anion**.
back: An **anion** is a negatively charged ion formed when a non-metal atom **gains** one or more electrons during ionic bond formation.

front: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
back: The **electrostatic attractions** between oppositely charged ions in the lattice act in all directions and are very strong. A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these forces, resulting in high melting points.

front:
**True or False?**

The ionic bond acts only between two specific oppositely charged ions.
back:
**False.**

The ionic bond acts in **all directions**. Each ion is attracted to all surrounding oppositely charged ions in the lattice.

front: In potassium chloride, the potassium atom **..........**  one electron to form a **..........**  ion, and the chlorine atom **..........**  that electron to form a chloride ion.
back: In potassium chloride, the potassium atom **loses** one electron to form a **K**<sup>**+**</sup> ion, and the chlorine atom **gains** that electron to form a chloride ion.

front: How can you use the periodic table to predict the charge on an ion formed by ionic bonding?
back: The **group number** indicates how many electrons a metal loses (for Groups 1 and 2) or how many a non-metal gains (for Groups 6 and 7), giving the ion charge. For example, Group 2 metals lose 2 electrons to form 2+ cations.

front: What ions are formed when sodium and chlorine react, and what is the formula of the ionic compound produced?
back: Sodium loses 1 electron to form Na<sup>+</sup> and chlorine gains 1 electron to form Cl<sup>-</sup>. The ionic compound formed is **NaCl** (sodium chloride).

front:
**True or False?**

In magnesium oxide, magnesium forms a 2+ ion and oxygen forms a 2- ion.
back:
**True.**

Magnesium (Group 2) loses 2 electrons to form Mg<sup>2+</sup> and oxygen (Group 6) gains 2 electrons to form O<sup>2-</sup>, giving the neutral compound MgO.

front: In calcium fluoride, one Ca<sup>2+</sup> ion bonds with **..........**  F<sup>-</sup> ions because each fluorine can only accept **..........**  electron, giving the formula **..........**  .
back: In calcium fluoride, one Ca<sup>2+</sup> ion bonds with **two** F<sup>-</sup> ions because each fluorine can only accept **one** electron, giving the formula **CaF**<sub>**2**</sub>.

front: Define **dot and cross diagram**.
back: A **dot and cross diagram** is a representation of ionic or covalent bonding in which electrons from different atoms are shown as dots or crosses, indicating which atom each electron originated from.

front: How many lithium ions are needed to form lithium nitride (Li<sub>3</sub>N), and why?
back: **Three** Li<sup>+</sup> ions are needed because nitrogen gains 3 electrons to form N<sup>3-</sup>, and each lithium can only donate 1 electron. Three Li<sup>+</sup> ions balance the 3- charge of one N<sup>3-</sup> ion.

front:
**True or False?**

Aluminium oxide has the formula AlO.
back:
**False.**

Aluminium forms Al<sup>3+</sup> and oxygen forms O<sup>2-</sup>. To balance the charges, 2 Al<sup>3+</sup> ions and 3 O<sup>2-</sup> ions are needed, giving the formula **Al**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**<sub>**3**</sub>.

front: In ionic bonding, the final ionic solid is always electrically **..........**  because positive and negative charges **..........**  each other.
back: In ionic bonding, the final ionic solid is always electrically **neutral** because positive and negative charges **cancel** each other.

front: What charge does the ion formed by a Group 7 non-metal carry, and why?
back: A Group 7 non-metal carries a **1- charge** because it needs to gain **1 electron** to achieve a full outer shell (8 electrons), matching the configuration of the nearest noble gas.

front:
**True or False?**

In NaCl, both the Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> ions adopt the electronic configuration of argon.
back:
**False.**

Na<sup>+</sup> has configuration [2,8] matching **neon**, while Cl<sup>-</sup> has configuration [2,8,8] matching **argon**. They adopt different noble gas configurations, not both argon.

front: Define **metallic bonding**.
back: **Metallic bonding** is the strong electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a surrounding sea of mobile delocalised electrons.

front: What happens to the outer electrons of metal atoms when they pack together to form a metallic lattice?
back: The outer electrons **delocalise**, becoming free to move throughout the structure. They are no longer associated with any single atom, forming a mobile 'sea' of electrons surrounding the positive metal ions.

front:
**True or False?**

In metallic bonding, the metal atoms remain neutral and do not form ions.
back:
**False.**

When outer electrons delocalise, the metal atoms become **positive ions** (cations). The structure consists of a lattice of these cations surrounded by delocalised electrons.

front: Metallic bonding holds the positive metal ions in place and counteracts the **..........**  between them, maintaining the **..........**  of the metal structure.
back: Metallic bonding holds the positive metal ions in place and counteracts the **repulsion** between them, maintaining the **stability** of the metal structure.

front: Describe the arrangement of particles in a metallic lattice.
back: Metal atoms are arranged in a **regular, tightly packed lattice**. Delocalisation of outer electrons produces a lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a mobile sea of delocalised electrons.

front:
**True or False?**

The delocalised electrons in metallic bonding are fixed to specific metal ions.
back:
**False.**

Delocalised electrons are **free to move** throughout the entire metallic lattice and are not associated with any single ion.

front: In a metal, delocalised electrons form a mobile '**..........**' that surrounds the **..........**  metal ions in the lattice.
back: In a metal, delocalised electrons form a mobile '**sea**' that surrounds the **positive** metal ions in the lattice.

front: Define **delocalised electrons**.
back: **Delocalised electrons** are electrons that are not associated with any single atom or bond but are free to move throughout a structure, as seen in metals and some covalent molecules.

front: Why is metallic bonding described as strong?
back: Metallic bonding is strong because the **electrostatic attraction** between the lattice of positive metal ions and the surrounding delocalised electrons acts in all directions and requires a large amount of energy to overcome.

front: Define **covalent bond**.
back: A **covalent bond** is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of two non-metal atoms and their shared pair of electrons in the outer shell.

front: How many electrons are shared in a single, double and triple covalent bond?
back: A **single** bond shares **2** electrons (1 pair), a **double** bond shares **4** electrons (2 pairs), and a **triple** bond shares **6** electrons (3 pairs).

front:
**True or False?**

In covalent bonding, electrons are transferred from one atom to the other.
back:
**False.**

In covalent bonding, electrons are **shared** between the two atoms. Electron transfer occurs in ionic bonding, not covalent bonding.

front: In N<sub>2</sub>, the two nitrogen atoms share **..........**  pairs of electrons, forming a **..........**  covalent bond.
back: In N<sub>2</sub>, the two nitrogen atoms share **three** pairs of electrons, forming a **triple** covalent bond.

front: What is meant by 'expanding the octet rule', and give one example?
back: Expanding the octet means a central atom accommodates **more than 8 electrons** in its outer shell. For example, sulfur in SF<sub>6</sub> has a share of **12 electrons**, forming six single S-F bonds.

front:
**True or False?**

Covalent bonding can occur between a metal and a non-metal.
back:
**False.**

Covalent bonding occurs between **two non-metals**. Bonding between a metal and a non-metal typically involves ionic bonding.

front: In a dot and cross diagram, **..........**  represent electrons from one atom and **..........**  represent electrons from the other atom, and only **..........**  shell electrons are shown.
back: In a dot and cross diagram, **dots** represent electrons from one atom and **crosses** represent electrons from the other atom, and only **outer** shell electrons are shown.

front: Why does PCl<sub>5</sub> have an expanded octet, and how many electrons does phosphorus share in this molecule?
back: Phosphorus uses available d orbitals to accommodate more than 8 electrons. In PCl<sub>5</sub>, phosphorus forms **5 single bonds** and has a share of **10 electrons**, exceeding the normal octet.

front:
**True or False?**

Sharing electrons in a covalent bond allows each atom to achieve a noble gas electron configuration.
back:
**True.**

Sharing electrons gives each atom a full outer shell similar to a noble gas configuration, increasing the stability of both atoms.

front: Define **coordinate bond**.
back: A **coordinate bond** (dative covalent bond) is a covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair are donated by the same atom, which must possess a lone pair.

front: How is the ammonium ion (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) formed, and which atom provides both electrons in the coordinate bond?
back: The **nitrogen** atom in ammonia donates its lone pair of electrons to the electron-deficient H<sup>+</sup> ion, forming a coordinate bond. Both electrons in this bond come from the nitrogen atom, producing NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>.

front:
**True or False?**

In a coordinate bond, the two electrons are contributed one from each atom.
back:
**False.**

In a coordinate bond, **both electrons** come from the **same atom** (the donor). This distinguishes it from an ordinary covalent bond.

front: At lower temperatures, two molecules of AlCl<sub>3</sub> join to form the **..........**  Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>, in which two **..........**  atoms each donate a lone pair to an aluminium atom.
back: At lower temperatures, two molecules of AlCl<sub>3</sub> join to form the **dimer** Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>, in which two **chlorine** atoms each donate a lone pair to an aluminium atom.

front: Define **electron-deficient atom**.
back: An **electron-deficient atom** is an atom that has an unfilled outer orbital and can therefore accept a lone pair of electrons to form a coordinate bond.

front: Why does AlCl<sub>3</sub> form a dimer (Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>) at lower temperatures?
back: AlCl<sub>3</sub> is **electron-deficient** (aluminium has an incomplete outer shell). At lower temperatures, lone pairs on chlorine atoms of one AlCl<sub>3</sub> molecule form **two coordinate bonds** with aluminium atoms of a second AlCl<sub>3</sub> molecule, giving the more stable dimer Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>.

front:
**True or False?**

Once formed, a coordinate bond is identical in strength and properties to an ordinary covalent bond.
back:
**True.**

After formation, a coordinate bond is indistinguishable from an ordinary covalent bond. The distinction lies only in the origin of the electrons, not in the bond itself.

front: In a dot and cross diagram, a coordinate bond is shown as an **..........**  pointing from the **..........**  pair to the electron-deficient atom.
back: In a dot and cross diagram, a coordinate bond is shown as an **arrow** pointing from the **lone** pair to the electron-deficient atom.

front: What condition must an atom satisfy to act as an electron pair donor in a coordinate bond?
back: The atom must possess a **lone pair** of electrons (a non-bonding pair) in its outer shell that it can donate to an electron-deficient atom.

front: Define **hybridisation**.
back: **Hybridisation** is the mixing of atomic orbitals within the same shell to form new hybrid orbitals of equal energy, used to explain the bonding and geometry of covalent molecules.

front: What orbitals combine to form sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals, and what geometry do they produce?
back: One **s orbital** and three **p orbitals** mix to form four sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals. These arrange with **tetrahedral geometry**, giving bond angles of **109.5°** (e.g. in methane, CH<sub>4</sub>).

front:
**True or False?**

A sigma bond is formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals.
back:
**False.**

A **sigma (σ) bond** is formed by the **end-on (direct) overlap** of atomic orbitals. Sideways overlap of p orbitals forms a **pi (π) bond**.

front: In ethene, each carbon atom is **..........**  hybridised, uses **..........**  hybrid orbitals to form sigma bonds and one unhybridised **..........**  orbital to form a pi bond.
back: In ethene, each carbon atom is **sp**<sup>**2**</sup> hybridised, uses **three** hybrid orbitals to form sigma bonds and one unhybridised **p** orbital to form a pi bond.

front: Define **pi (π) bond**.
back: A **pi (π) bond** is formed by the sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals, with electron density distributed above and below the plane of the sigma bond.

front: How many sigma bonds and pi bonds are in a carbon-carbon triple bond (as in ethyne)?
back: A triple bond contains **one sigma (σ) bond** and **two pi (π) bonds**. The sigma bond arises from end-on overlap and the two pi bonds from sideways overlap of two pairs of p orbitals at right angles to each other.

front:
**True or False?**

sp hybridisation produces a linear geometry with a bond angle of 180°.
back:
**True.**

In sp hybridisation, one s and one p orbital mix to form two sp hybrid orbitals that arrange linearly, giving a bond angle of **180°** (e.g. in ethyne).

front: The **..........**  the orbital overlap in a covalent bond, the **..........**  the bond. Sigma bonds have **..........**  overlap than pi bonds.
back: The **greater** the orbital overlap in a covalent bond, the **stronger** the bond. Sigma bonds have **greater** overlap than pi bonds.

front: What hybridisation does nitrogen adopt in ammonia, and how does the lone pair affect the bond angle compared to methane?
back: Nitrogen in NH<sub>3</sub> is **sp**<sup>**3**</sup> hybridised. The lone pair occupies one sp<sup>3</sup> orbital and repels the bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other, reducing the bond angle to **107°** (compared to 109.5° in CH<sub>4</sub>).

front: Define **bond energy**.
back: **Bond energy** is the energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state, measured in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. A larger bond energy indicates a stronger bond.

front: Define **bond length**.
back: **Bond length** is the internuclear distance between two covalently bonded atoms, measured from the nucleus of one atom to the nucleus of the other.

front: How do bond length and bond energy compare for single, double and triple carbon-carbon bonds?
back: Going from single to triple bond: bond length **decreases** (single <sub>147 pm, double </sub>134 pm, triple <sub>120 pm) and bond energy </sub>**<sub>increases</sub>**<sub> (single </sub>347 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>, double <sub>614 kJ mol</sub><sup><sub>-1</sub></sup><sub>, triple </sub>839 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>). Triple bonds are the shortest and strongest.

front:
**True or False?**

A longer bond length corresponds to a stronger covalent bond.
back:
**False.**

A longer bond length means the nuclei are further apart and the attractive forces are weaker, so the bond is **weaker**. Shorter bonds are stronger.

front: Triple bonds have a **..........**  bond length and a **..........**  bond energy compared to single bonds, because the greater electron density **..........**  the forces of attraction between nuclei and electrons.
back: Triple bonds have a **shorter** bond length and a **higher** bond energy compared to single bonds, because the greater electron density **increases** the forces of attraction between nuclei and electrons.

front: Why does bond energy decrease in the order HCl > HBr > HI?
back: Going down the halogen group, the atoms become larger. The bonding electrons are further from the nucleus and experience greater shielding, so the **attractive force between bonding electrons and nucleus decreases**, making the bond easier to break.

front:
**True or False?**

HI is more reactive than HCl because it has a shorter bond length.
back:
**False.**

HI has a **longer** bond length (0.161 nm vs 0.127 nm for HCl) and a **lower** bond energy, meaning less energy is needed to break the bond, making HI **more reactive**.

front: The reactivity of a covalent bond is influenced by its **..........**  , its **..........**  and the bond **..........**  (sigma or pi).
back: The reactivity of a covalent bond is influenced by its **polarity**, its **strength** and the bond **type** (sigma or pi).

front: What units are used for bond energy, and what does a higher value tell you about the bond?
back: Bond energy is measured in **kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>. A higher value means the bond requires more energy to break, indicating a **stronger** covalent bond.

front: Define **VSEPR theory**.
back: **VSEPR theory** (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory) states that electron pairs around a central atom repel each other and arrange themselves as far apart as possible to minimise repulsion, determining the shape of the molecule.

front: State the three key rules of VSEPR theory.
back:
1. All **electron pairs** (bonding and lone pairs) spread out as far apart as possible.
2. **Lone pairs** repel more strongly than **bonding pairs**.
3. **Multiple bonds** behave like a single electron domain when determining shape.

front:
**True or False?**

Lone pairs repel neighbouring electron pairs more strongly than bonding pairs do.
back:
**True.**

Lone pairs are held closer to the nucleus and spread over a larger region of space, causing greater repulsion. This reduces bond angles compared to the regular geometry.

front: NH<sub>3</sub> has a **..........**  shape with a bond angle of **..........**  because one lone pair repels the bonding pairs, reducing the angle from 109.5°.
back: NH<sub>3</sub> has a **trigonal pyramidal** shape with a bond angle of **107°** because one lone pair repels the bonding pairs, reducing the angle from 109.5°.

front: What shape and bond angle does SF<sub>6</sub> adopt, and why?
back: SF<sub>6</sub> adopts an **octahedral** shape with bond angles of **90°**. Sulfur forms 6 single bonds with no lone pairs, so all six bonding pairs repel each other equally.

front:
**True or False?**

CO<sub>2</sub> has a bent shape because of lone pairs on the carbon atom.
back:
**False.**

CO<sub>2</sub> is **linear** (180°). Carbon has no lone pairs and forms two double bonds, each counted as one electron domain. The two domains arrange linearly.

front: PCl<sub>5</sub> has a **..........**  shape with bond angles of **..........**  (equatorial) and **..........**  (axial).
back: PCl<sub>5</sub> has a **trigonal bipyramidal** shape with bond angles of **120°** (equatorial) and **90°** (axial).

front: Why does H<sub>2</sub>O have a bond angle of 104.5° rather than the tetrahedral angle of 109.5°?
back: Oxygen in H<sub>2</sub>O has **two lone pairs** in addition to two bonding pairs. The lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, compressing the H-O-H bond angle from 109.5° to **104.5°**.

front:
**True or False?**

BF<sub>3</sub> has a trigonal planar shape with bond angles of 120°.
back:
**True.**

Boron forms 3 bonding pairs and has no lone pairs. The three electron domains arrange with **trigonal planar geometry**, giving bond angles of **120°**.

front: Define **hydrogen bond**.
back: A **hydrogen bond** is the strongest type of intermolecular force, formed between a highly polarised O-H, N-H or F-H bond and a lone pair on an O, N or F atom in an adjacent molecule.

front: State the two conditions required for hydrogen bonding to occur between molecules.
back:
1. A molecule must contain a highly **electronegative** atom (**O, N or F**) with a **lone pair** of electrons.
2. A hydrogen atom must be covalently bonded directly to **O, N or F**, making the bond highly **polar**.

front:
**True or False?**

Ice is denser than liquid water because the molecules in ice are more tightly packed.
back:
**False.**

Ice is **less dense** than liquid water. In ice, water molecules form a rigid open 3D hydrogen-bonded lattice with relatively long bond lengths, so the molecules are slightly further apart than in liquid water.

front: Each water molecule can form a maximum of **..........**  hydrogen bonds, because oxygen has **..........**  lone pairs and **..........**  polar O-H bonds.
back: Each water molecule can form a maximum of **four** hydrogen bonds, because oxygen has **two** lone pairs and **two** polar O-H bonds.

front: Why does water have a much higher enthalpy of vaporisation than expected from the trend in Group 16 hydrides?
back: The trend from H<sub>2</sub>S to H<sub>2</sub>Te suggests H<sub>2</sub>O should have an enthalpy of vaporisation of about 17 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. The actual value is almost three times larger because of the **additional energy needed to break hydrogen bonds** in water, which are absent in the other hydrides.

front:
**True or False?**

NH<sub>3</sub> can form more hydrogen bonds per molecule than H<sub>2</sub>O.
back:
**False.**

NH<sub>3</sub> can form up to **four** hydrogen bonds per molecule (one as acceptor via its lone pair on nitrogen, three as donors via N–H bonds) — the same maximum as H<sub>2</sub>O, not more. The statement is false because NH<sub>3</sub> cannot form **more** than H<sub>2</sub>O.

front: Hydrogen bonds are strongest when the angle between the covalent bond and the hydrogen bond is **..........**  because this **..........**  the electrostatic attraction.
back: Hydrogen bonds are strongest when the angle between the covalent bond and the hydrogen bond is **180°** because this **maximises** the electrostatic attraction.

front: Why does water have a high surface tension?
back: Surface molecules are pulled **downwards** by hydrogen bonds with interior molecules. This compresses and tightens the surface layer, resisting external forces. Interior molecules are pulled in all directions so the net force is zero.

front:
**True or False?**

Hydrogen bonding is the strongest type of intermolecular force.
back:
**True.**

Hydrogen bonding is the strongest intermolecular force. It is a special, stronger case of permanent dipole-permanent dipole interaction, arising when H is bonded directly to O, N or F.

front: Define **electronegativity**.
back: **Electronegativity** is the ability of an atom to draw a pair of electrons towards itself in a covalent bond.

front: How does electronegativity change across a Period and down a Group?
back: Electronegativity **increases** across a Period and **decreases** going down a Group.

front:
**True or False?**

A covalent bond between two atoms of the same element is polar.
back: **False.** When two atoms have the same electronegativity, the bonding electrons are shared equally and the bond is **nonpolar**.

front: In a polar covalent bond, the more electronegative atom gains a partial charge of **..........**  and the less electronegative atom gains a partial charge of **..........**.
back: In a polar covalent bond, the more electronegative atom gains a partial charge of **δ−** and the less electronegative atom gains a partial charge of **δ+**.

front: Define **dipole moment**.
back: A **dipole moment** is a measure of how polar a bond is. The arrow representing it points towards the δ− end of the dipole.

front: What two factors must be considered when deciding whether a molecule with more than two atoms is polar overall?
back:
1. The **polarity of each bond** in the molecule.
2. The **arrangement** of those bonds — if individual dipole moments cancel each other out, the molecule is nonpolar overall.

front:
**True or False?**

CCl<sub>4</sub> is a polar molecule because it contains four polar C–Cl bonds.
back: **False.** Although CCl<sub>4</sub> contains four polar C–Cl bonds, the individual dipole moments cancel each other out due to the symmetrical tetrahedral arrangement, making CCl<sub>4</sub> a **nonpolar** molecule.

front: The greater the difference in **..........**  between two bonded atoms, the more **..........**  the bond becomes.
back: The greater the difference in **electronegativity** between two bonded atoms, the more **polar** the bond becomes.

front: Explain why CH<sub>3</sub>Cl is a polar molecule but CCl<sub>4</sub> is not, even though both contain polar C–Cl bonds.
back: In CH<sub>3</sub>Cl the four polar bonds (three C–H and one C–Cl) do not cancel each other out, giving a **net dipole** towards the electronegative Cl atom. In CCl<sub>4</sub> the four identical C–Cl bond dipoles are arranged **symmetrically** and cancel each other out, so there is no overall dipole.

front: Define **van der Waals' forces**.
back: **Van der Waals' forces** are weak intermolecular forces between molecules. They include instantaneous dipole – induced dipole forces (London dispersion forces) and permanent dipole – permanent dipole forces.

front: What causes an instantaneous dipole to form in a non-polar molecule?
back: The electron charge cloud is constantly moving. At any moment it can be more concentrated on one side of the molecule than the other, creating a **temporary uneven distribution of charge** — an instantaneous dipole.

front:
**True or False?**

Instantaneous dipole – induced dipole forces exist only between polar molecules.
back: **False.** London dispersion forces exist between **all** atoms and molecules, including non-polar ones.

front: Id–id forces increase with an increasing number of **..........**  in the molecule and with increasing **..........**  where molecules come close together.
back: Id–id forces increase with an increasing number of **electrons** in the molecule and with increasing **contact points** where molecules come close together.

front: Define **permanent dipole – permanent dipole forces**.
back: **Permanent dipole – permanent dipole forces** are the attractive intermolecular forces between the δ+ end of one polar molecule and the δ− end of a neighbouring polar molecule.

front: Propanone has a higher boiling point than butane, even though both molecules have the same number of electrons. Explain why.
back: Propanone is polar so it has **permanent dipole – permanent dipole forces** between its molecules. Butane is non-polar and only has weaker id–id forces.
