back: Chain isomerism arises from **branching** in the carbon skeleton, which changes the length of the longest chain even though the molecular formula remains the same.

front: Define **stereoisomers**.
back: **Stereoisomers** are compounds with the same atoms connected to each other in the same order but with those atoms **differently arranged in space**.

front: What are the two types of stereoisomerism?
back: The two types are **geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism** and **optical isomerism**.

front:
**True or False?**

In a cis isomer, the two identical functional groups are on opposite sides of the double bond.
back:
**False.**

In a **cis** isomer, identical functional groups are on the **same side** of the double bond. In a **trans** isomer, they are on opposite sides.

front: Define **enantiomers**.
back: **Enantiomers** are the two optical isomers of a chiral molecule. They are **non-superimposable mirror images** of each other.

front: Geometrical isomerism in alkenes arises because the **..........**  bond prevents **..........**  rotation about the C=C bond, fixing the groups in position.
back: Geometrical isomerism in alkenes arises because the **π** bond prevents **free** rotation about the C=C bond, fixing the groups in position.

front: How do enantiomers differ from each other in their interaction with polarised light?
back: One enantiomer rotates the plane of polarised light **clockwise** and the other rotates it **anticlockwise**. They rotate it by the same angle but in opposite directions.

front:
**True or False?**

Geometrical isomerism can occur in cyclic compounds as well as in alkenes.
back:
**True.**

In cyclic compounds, limited rotation about the C–C bonds that make up the ring fixes substituents either above or below the ring, giving rise to cis/trans **geometrical isomers**.

front: Geometrical and optical isomers are both types of **..........**  isomerism. They differ from **..........**  isomers, which have different structural formulae.
back: Geometrical and optical isomers are both types of **stereo** isomerism. They differ from **structural** isomers, which have different structural formulae.

front: Why does free rotation about a C=C double bond not occur, but free rotation about a C–C single bond does?
back: Rotation about a C=C bond would break the **π bond** (which requires energy to re-form), so it does not occur freely. A C–C single bond has only a **σ bond**, which allows free rotation.

front: Define **chiral centre**.
back: A **chiral centre** is a carbon atom bonded to **four different** atoms or groups of atoms, giving rise to two non-superimposable mirror image optical isomers.

front: How many optical isomers can a molecule with two chiral centres form?
back: A molecule with two chiral centres can form up to **four** optical isomers (2<sup>2</sup> = 4). The maximum number of stereoisomers is **2**<sup>**n**</sup>, where n is the number of chiral centres.

front:
**True or False?**

Enantiomers are superimposable mirror images of each other.
back:
**False.**

Enantiomers are **non-superimposable** mirror images. Just as a left hand cannot be placed exactly over a right hand, one enantiomer cannot be superimposed on the other.

front: Define **chiral molecule**.
back: A **chiral molecule** is a molecule that contains one or more chiral centres and therefore exists as two non-superimposable mirror image forms (enantiomers).

front: The maximum number of stereoisomers for a molecule with n chiral centres is **..........** . A molecule with three chiral centres can have a maximum of **..........**  stereoisomers.
back: The maximum number of stereoisomers for a molecule with n chiral centres is **2****<sup>n</sup>**. A molecule with three chiral centres can have a maximum of **eight** stereoisomers.

front: How do you identify a chiral centre in a cyclic molecule?
back: Find the carbon atom in the ring that is bonded to **four different** atoms or groups of atoms. The two ring bonds count as different groups if the atoms on each side of the ring differ.

front:
**True or False?**

A molecule with one chiral centre always produces exactly two optical isomers.
back:
**True.**

One chiral centre gives 2<sup>1</sup> = **two** optical isomers (enantiomers), which are mirror images of each other.

front: To identify a chiral centre, look for a carbon bonded to **..........**  different atoms or groups. Such a molecule is described as **..........**  and has no plane of symmetry.
back: To identify a chiral centre, look for a carbon bonded to **four** different atoms or groups. Such a molecule is described as **chiral** and has no plane of symmetry.

front: What is the key condition for geometrical isomerism to occur in a molecule?
back: Geometrical isomerism requires **restricted rotation** about a C–C bond (as in alkenes or cyclic compounds) AND **different groups** attached to each carbon of the restricted bond.

front: What is the systematic approach for deducing all possible isomers of an organic compound?
back:
1. Draw the structural formula.
2. Decide whether **stereoisomerism** or **structural isomerism** applies.
3. For structural isomers, check for **chain**, **positional** and **functional group** types. For stereoisomers, check for **geometrical (cis/trans)** and **optical** types.

front:
**True or False?**

C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> has only one possible structural isomer.
back:
**False.**

C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> has **two** structural isomers: **butane** (straight chain) and **2-methylpropane** (branched chain). These are chain isomers.

front: Define **positional isomer**.
back: A **positional isomer** is a structural isomer in which the same functional group is located on a **different carbon** of the same parent chain.

front: How many structural isomers does C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>Br<sub>2</sub> (dibromopropane) have and what type of isomerism do they show?
back: Dibromopropane has **four** structural isomers: 1,1-dibromopropane, 2,2-dibromopropane, 1,2-dibromopropane and 1,3-dibromopropane. These are all **positional** isomers.

front: 1,1-dichloroethene is a **..........**  isomer of 1,2-dichloroethene. However, only **..........**  exhibits geometrical isomerism because it has restricted rotation and two different groups on each C=C carbon.
back: 1,1-dichloroethene is a **structural** isomer of 1,2-dichloroethene. However, only **1,2-dichloroethene** exhibits geometrical isomerism because it has restricted rotation and two different groups on each C=C carbon.

front:
**True or False?**

A compound with no restricted bond rotation and no chiral centre can exhibit stereoisomerism.
back:
**False.**

Stereoisomerism requires either **restricted rotation** (for geometrical isomers) or a **chiral centre** (for optical isomers). Without either, only structural isomers are possible.

front: To deduce if geometrical isomerism is possible, first check for **..........**  rotation about a C=C or ring bond, then check that each carbon of the double bond has **..........**  groups attached.
back: To deduce if geometrical isomerism is possible, first check for **restricted** rotation about a C=C or ring bond, then check that each carbon of the double bond has **two different** groups attached.

front: What two conditions must both be met for a molecule to show geometrical isomerism?
back:
1. There must be **restricted rotation** about a C=C bond or within a ring.
2. Each carbon involved in the restricted bond must have **two different groups** attached.

front:
**True or False?**

Chain isomerism arises when the same molecular formula can give molecules with different numbers of carbons in the longest chain.
back:
**True.**

**Chain isomers** have the same molecular formula but different carbon chain lengths due to branching. For example, butane and 2-methylpropane are both C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>.

front: Define **hydrogenation**.
back: **Hydrogenation** is the addition reaction of an alkene with hydrogen gas in the presence of a finely divided Pt or Ni catalyst to produce an **alkane**.

front: What conditions are required for the hydrogenation of an alkene to form an alkane?
back: Hydrogen gas, heat, and a finely divided **Pt** or **Ni** catalyst are required. The catalyst is finely divided to increase its surface area and raise the rate of reaction.

front:
**True or False?**

Hydrogenation of an alkene is an endothermic reaction.
back: **False.** Hydrogenation is an **exothermic** reaction. Cracking, by contrast, is endothermic.

front: In the manufacture of margarine, vegetable oil is partially **..........**ed so that C=C double bonds are reduced, making the hydrocarbon chains straighter and raising the **..........**.
back: In the manufacture of margarine, vegetable oil is partially **hydrogenat**ed so that C=C double bonds are reduced, making the hydrocarbon chains straighter and raising the **melting point**.

front: What type of molecules are produced when a large alkane is cracked?
back: Cracking produces a **smaller alkane** and an **alkene**. For example, decane (C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>22</sub>) can be cracked to give octane (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>) and ethene (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>).

front:
**True or False?**

The cracking chamber contains oxygen to combust the hydrocarbon and release energy.
back: **False.** The chamber contains **no oxygen**. Oxygen would cause the hydrocarbon to combust to water and carbon dioxide rather than cracking into smaller molecules.

front: In cracking, large hydrocarbon molecules are heated in a steel chamber and passed over an **..........** catalyst to break them into smaller molecules.
back: In cracking, large hydrocarbon molecules are heated in a steel chamber and passed over an **aluminium oxide (Al**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**<sub>**3**</sub>**)** catalyst to break them into smaller molecules.

front: Define **cracking**.
back: **Cracking** is the process in which large, less useful hydrocarbon molecules from crude oil are broken down into smaller, more useful **alkane** and **alkene** molecules using heat and an Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> catalyst.

front: Why is the Pt or Ni catalyst used in hydrogenation finely divided?
back: The catalyst is finely divided to **increase its surface area**, which increases the overall rate of the hydrogenation reaction.

front: What products are formed during the complete combustion of an alkane?
back: Complete combustion of an alkane produces **carbon dioxide** and **water**. All the carbon and hydrogen are fully oxidised. This requires a plentiful supply of oxygen.

front:
**True or False?**

Carbon monoxide is produced during the complete combustion of an alkane.
back: **False.** Carbon monoxide is produced during **incomplete** combustion, which occurs when the oxygen supply is limited. Complete combustion produces carbon dioxide.

front: Define **incomplete combustion**.
back: **Incomplete combustion** is the burning of a hydrocarbon in a limited supply of oxygen, where carbon is only partially oxidised to form **carbon monoxide** rather than carbon dioxide.

front: Carbon monoxide is toxic because it binds to **..........**in blood, preventing it from carrying **..........** around the body.
back: Carbon monoxide is toxic because it binds to **haemoglobin** in blood, preventing it from carrying **oxygen** around the body.

front: Why is carbon monoxide particularly dangerous as a toxic gas?
back: Carbon monoxide is **odourless** and therefore cannot be detected by smell. It binds to haemoglobin in the blood, preventing oxygen transport, and can cause dizziness, loss of consciousness and death.

front:
**True or False?**

Ultraviolet light is required to initiate free-radical substitution of alkanes.
back: **True.** Alkanes are very unreactive and UV light provides the energy needed to break the halogen bond (Cl–Cl or Br–Br) in the initiation step.

front: In free-radical substitution, a hydrogen atom on an alkane is substituted by a **..........** The three steps of the mechanism are **..........**,  propagation and termination.
back: In free-radical substitution, a hydrogen atom on an alkane is substituted by a **halogen**. The three steps of the mechanism are **initiation**, propagation and termination.

front: Define **termination step**.
back: A **termination step** is the final stage of free-radical substitution in which two **radicals** collide and combine, ending the chain reaction.

front: What happens in the initiation step of free-radical substitution?
back: The halogen–halogen bond (e.g. Cl–Cl or Br–Br) is broken by **UV energy** to produce two halogen **radicals**. These radicals then drive the propagation steps of the chain reaction.

front: Define **homolytic fission**.
back: **Homolytic fission** is the breaking of a covalent bond in which each atom takes **one electron** from the shared pair, producing two **radicals**.

front: What is produced in the initiation step of free-radical substitution of chlorine with an alkane?
back: UV energy causes **homolytic fission** of the Cl–Cl bond, producing two **chlorine radicals** (Cl<sup>•</sup>). Each chlorine atom takes one electron from the bond.

front:
**True or False?**

In the propagation step, the chlorine radical is consumed and not regenerated.
back: **False.** The chlorine radical is **regenerated** in the second propagation step when an alkyl radical reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub>, producing the halogenoalkane and a new Cl<sup>•</sup> radical.

front: In the termination step of free-radical substitution, two **..........** collide and combine to form a single **..........** molecule, ending the chain reaction.
back: In the termination step of free-radical substitution, two **radicals** collide and combine to form a single **unreactive** molecule, ending the chain reaction.

front: Why is free-radical substitution not a good method for preparing a specific halogenoalkane?
back: A **mixture** of substitution products is formed. If excess halogen is present, all hydrogen atoms can eventually be substituted, giving a range of products rather than one specific compound.

front:
**True or False?**

Half-headed (fish hook) arrows are used in free-radical mechanisms to show the movement of a single electron.
back: **True.** Half-headed arrows show the movement of **one electron**. Double-headed (curly) arrows show the movement of an electron pair and are used in ionic mechanisms.

front: In the chlorination of methane, complete substitution produces **..........**. The intermediate after three substitutions is **..........** (CHCl<sub>3</sub>).
back: In the chlorination of methane, complete substitution produces **CCl**<sub>**4**</sub>. The intermediate after three substitutions is **trichloromethane** (CHCl<sub>3</sub>).

front: Define **propagation step**.
back: A **propagation step** is the repeating stage of free-radical substitution in which a **radical** reacts with the alkane to form an alkyl radical and HX, then the alkyl radical reacts with X<sub>2</sub> to regenerate the **halogen radical**.

front: In the termination step, give one example of a product other than the expected halogenoalkane that can form.
back: Two alkyl radicals can combine to form a **longer alkane**. For example, two ethyl radicals (<sup>•</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) combine to give **butane** (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>).

front: Define **crude oil**.
back: **Crude oil** is a mixture of hydrocarbons — including **alkanes**, cycloalkanes and arenes — extracted from the earth by drilling and refined by fractional distillation.

front: Why are heavier fractions from fractional distillation subjected to cracking?
back: The smaller hydrocarbon fractions such as **gasoline** are in high demand, but heavier fractions are in excess. Cracking breaks these down into smaller, more useful **alkanes** and **alkenes** with lower ***M***<sub>r</sub> values.

front: In cracking, large hydrocarbon molecules are heated in a steel chamber and passed over **..........** catalyst. Oxygen is excluded to prevent **..........** of the hydrocarbons.
back: In cracking, large hydrocarbon molecules are heated in a steel chamber and passed over **aluminium oxide (Al**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**<sub>**3**</sub>**)** catalyst. Oxygen is excluded to prevent **combustion** of the hydrocarbons.

front:
**True or False?**

Fractional distillation of crude oil separates hydrocarbons based on their molecular mass only.
back: **False.** Fractional distillation separates hydrocarbons based on their **boiling points**. Boiling point is related to molecular mass, but it is boiling point that determines the separation into fractions.

front: Why are the low-molecular-mass alkenes formed in cracking particularly valuable to the chemical industry?
back: Alkenes are more **reactive** than alkanes due to their C=C double bond. This makes them useful **feedstock** — for example, as monomers in polymerisation reactions and as starting compounds for many other syntheses.

front:
**True or False?**

Cracking of decane (C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>22</sub>) can produce octane and ethene.
back: **True.** Decane (C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>22</sub>) can be cracked to give **octane** (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>) and **ethene** (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>) — a smaller alkane and an alkene.

front: Define **feedstock**.
back: A **feedstock** is a raw material used as the starting compound for an industrial chemical process. Alkenes from cracking are valuable **feedstocks** for polymerisation and other synthesis reactions.

front: Crude oil contains **..........**,  cycloalkanes and **..........**  (compounds with a benzene ring).
back: Crude oil contains **alkanes**, cycloalkanes and **arenes** (compounds with a benzene ring).

front: What two types of organic product are always formed when a large alkane is cracked?
back: Cracking always produces a **smaller alkane** and an **alkene**. The alkane fraction makes a useful fuel and the alkene is reactive enough to be used as a chemical feedstock.

front: Give two reasons why alkanes are chemically unreactive.
back:
1. Alkanes have **strong C–C and C–H covalent bonds** that require a lot of energy to break.
2. Alkanes are **nonpolar** molecules, so they do not react with polar reagents, nucleophiles or electrophiles.

front:
**True or False?**

Alkanes are polar molecules because carbon is more electronegative than hydrogen.
back: **False.** Although carbon is slightly more electronegative than hydrogen (difference of only **0.4** on the Pauling scale), alkanes are considered **nonpolar** molecules. There are no significant partial charges on the C–H or C–C bonds.

front: Define **nucleophile**.
back: A **nucleophile** is a species that is attracted to **electron-deficient** regions. Alkanes do not react with nucleophiles because they have no electron-deficient areas.

front: Alkanes do not react with polar reagents because they are **..........**  molecules and have no **..........**  or electrophilic sites.
back: Alkanes do not react with polar reagents because they are **nonpolar** molecules and have no **nucleophilic** or electrophilic sites.

front:
**True or False?**

Alkanes can react with electrophiles because they have electron-rich areas in the C–H bonds.
back: **False.** Alkanes lack electron-rich areas to attract **electrophiles**. They are nonpolar, so neither electrophiles nor nucleophiles are drawn to them.

front: What are the only two types of reaction that alkanes typically undergo?
back: Alkanes undergo **combustion** (complete and incomplete) and **free-radical substitution** with halogens. Their strong, nonpolar bonds make them resistant to all other reaction types.

front: The difference in electronegativity between carbon and hydrogen is only **..........** on the Pauling scale, which means C–H bonds are essentially **..........** .
back: The difference in electronegativity between carbon and hydrogen is only **0.4** on the Pauling scale, which means C–H bonds are essentially **nonpolar**.

front: Define **electrophile**.
back: An **electrophile** is a species that is attracted to **electron-rich** regions. Alkanes do not react with electrophiles because they have no areas of high electron density.

front: Why do strong C–C and C–H bonds reduce the reactivity of alkanes?
back: A large amount of **energy** is required to break these strong bonds. Because the activation energy is high and there are no weak or polar bonds to facilitate attack, alkanes rarely react under mild conditions.

front: Define **photochemical smog**.
back: **Photochemical smog** is an atmospheric pollutant formed when volatile organic compounds (VOCs) react with **oxides of nitrogen** in sunlight to produce **peroxyacetyl nitrate** (PAN), which is harmful to the lungs, eyes and plant life.

front: Why is carbon monoxide particularly dangerous as an exhaust gas pollutant?
back: Carbon monoxide is **colourless** and **odourless**, so it cannot be detected without a sensor. It binds to **haemoglobin** with very high affinity (much higher than O<sub>2</sub>), preventing oxygen transport, and can cause dizziness, loss of consciousness and death.

front:
**True or False?**

Nitrogen is reactive enough to combine with oxygen under normal atmospheric conditions.
back: **False.** Nitrogen is normally too **unreactive** to oxidise under atmospheric conditions. It only reacts with oxygen inside a car engine where the **high temperatures and pressures** are sufficient to drive the reaction.

front: Oxides of nitrogen from car exhaust dissolve in water and react with oxygen to form **..........**,  a cause of **..........** rain.
back: Oxides of nitrogen from car exhaust dissolve in water and react with oxygen to form **nitric acid**, a cause of **acid** rain.

front: How does a catalytic converter reduce pollutants from car exhaust fumes?
back: Precious metals (e.g. **platinum**) coated on a honeycomb structure provide a large surface area. CO is **oxidised** to CO<sub>2</sub> and NO/NO<sub>2</sub> is **reduced** to N<sub>2</sub>. Unburnt hydrocarbons (VOCs) are also oxidised to CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O.

front:
**True or False?**

Carbon dioxide is a toxic gas and a pollutant that causes direct harm to human health.
back: **False.** CO<sub>2</sub> is **not toxic** but it is still a **pollutant** that contributes to **global warming** and climate change. It is CO (carbon monoxide) that is directly toxic.

front: In a catalytic converter, the reaction **2CO + 2NO → **..........**  + N****<sub>2</sub>** simultaneously removes **..........** and nitrogen monoxide.
back: In a catalytic converter, the reaction **2CO + 2NO → 2CO**<sub>**2**</sub> + N<sub>2</sub> simultaneously removes **carbon monoxide** and nitrogen monoxide.

front: Define **volatile organic compounds (VOCs)**.
back: **Volatile organic compounds (VOCs)** are unburnt hydrocarbons and their oxides released in car exhaust fumes. They react with **oxides of nitrogen** in sunlight to produce PAN, contributing to photochemical smog.

front: What are the three main types of pollutant found in car exhaust fumes and what is one environmental consequence of each?
back:
1. **Carbon monoxide (CO)** — toxic; prevents oxygen transport in blood.
2. **Oxides of nitrogen (NO/NO**<sub>**2**</sub>**)** — form nitric acid; cause acid rain.
3. **VOCs** — react with NOx to form PAN; contribute to photochemical smog.

front: What are the three methods by which alkenes can be produced?
back:
Alkenes can be produced by:

1. **Elimination** reaction of a halogenoalkane with ethanolic NaOH.
2. **Dehydration** of an alcohol using a hot Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> catalyst.
3. **Cracking** of long-chain hydrocarbons from crude oil.

front:
**True or False?**

Reacting a halogenoalkane with aqueous NaOH produces an alkene.
back: **False.** Aqueous NaOH causes **nucleophilic substitution** to produce an **alcohol**. Ethanolic NaOH (NaOH dissolved in ethanol) is needed for the **elimination** reaction that produces an alkene.

front: Define **dehydration reaction**.
back: A **dehydration reaction** is an elimination reaction in which a **water** molecule is lost from an alcohol to produce an **alkene**, using a hot Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> catalyst or concentrated acid.

front: In the elimination of a halogenoalkane, the small molecule lost is **..........** The reagent used is **..........** sodium hydroxide.
back: In the elimination of a halogenoalkane, the small molecule lost is **hydrogen halide (HX)**. The reagent used is **ethanolic** sodium hydroxide.

front:
**True or False?**

Small alkenes such as ethene are gases at room temperature and can be collected over water.
back: **True.** Small alkenes including ethene, propene and butene are **gaseous** at room temperature. They are collected by displacement of water in an inverted container.

front: What catalyst and conditions are used to dehydrate an alcohol to form an alkene?
back: Alcohol vapour is passed over a **hot** catalyst of **aluminium oxide (Al**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**<sub>**3**</sub>**) powder**. Concentrated acid or porous pot can also be used as alternative catalysts.

front: When bromoethane reacts with ethanolic NaOH, the Br<sup>-</sup> ion reacts with Na<sup>+</sup> to form **..........**,  and the H<sup>+</sup> reacts with OH<sup>-</sup> to form **..........** .
back: When bromoethane reacts with ethanolic NaOH, the Br<sup>-</sup> ion reacts with Na<sup>+</sup> to form **NaBr**, and the H<sup>+</sup> reacts with OH<sup>-</sup> to form **water**.

front: Define **elimination reaction**.
back: An **elimination reaction** is one in which a **small molecule** is removed from a larger molecule. In organic chemistry, it converts a halogenoalkane or alcohol into an **alkene** by losing HX or H<sub>2</sub>O respectively.

front: Why must oxygen be excluded during cracking of crude oil?
back: Oxygen would cause **combustion** of the hydrocarbons, producing CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O rather than the desired smaller alkane and **alkene** molecules.

front: Define **electrophilic addition**.
back: **Electrophilic addition** is the addition of an **electrophile** across a C=C double bond in an alkene, breaking the double bond and forming two new single bonds.

front: What product is formed when an alkene is shaken with cold dilute acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>?
back: A **diol** is formed. The pale purple KMnO<sub>4</sub> solution turns **colourless** as the alkene is oxidised, with an OH group added to each of the two carbon atoms of the double bond.

front:
**True or False?**

Hot concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> always produces a diol from an alkene.
back: **False.** Hot concentrated KMnO<sub>4</sub> causes the C=C bond to **completely break**, producing ketones, aldehydes, carboxylic acids or CO<sub>2</sub>, depending on the substitution pattern. **Diols** are only formed with cold dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub>.

front: In addition polymerisation, the **..........**  double bond in many monomer molecules is broken to link them into a long-chain **..........**.
back: In addition polymerisation, the **C=C** double bond in many monomer molecules is broken to link them into a long-chain **polymer**.

front: Name four electrophilic addition reactions that alkenes can undergo.
back:
Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition with:

1. **Hydrogen** (hydrogenation).
2. **Steam** (H<sub>2</sub>O (g)) to form an alcohol.
3. **Hydrogen halide** (HX) to form a halogenoalkane.
4. **Halogen** (X<sub>2</sub>) to form a dihalide.

front:
**True or False?**

Oxidation of an alkene with hot concentrated KMnO<sub>4</sub> can be used to identify the position of the double bond.
back: **True.** The products of hot concentrated KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidation depend on the groups attached to each carbon in the double bond, which allows the **position** of the C=C to be deduced from the products formed.

front: Define **addition polymerisation**.
back: **Addition polymerisation** is the reaction of many alkene **monomers** through their C=C double bonds to form a long-chain **polymer** as the only product.

front: When a carbon in an alkene's double bond carries **two alkyl groups**, hot concentrated KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidation produces a **..........** . When it carries one H and one alkyl group, a **..........**  is produced.
back: When a carbon in an alkene's double bond carries two alkyl groups, hot concentrated KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidation produces a **ketone**. When it carries one H and one alkyl group, a **carboxylic acid** is produced.

front: What is poly(chloroethene) (PVC) and how is it made?
back: Poly(chloroethene) (PVC) is made by the **addition polymerisation** of chloroethene monomers. The C=C double bonds break and the monomers link together, forming a versatile plastic polymer.

front: What is the reagent used to test for unsaturation in an organic compound, and what is the observation if unsaturation is present?
back: **Bromine water** (Br<sub>2</sub> (aq)) is used. If the compound is unsaturated, the orange/yellow solution **decolourises** as bromine undergoes an addition reaction across the C=C double bond.

front:
**True or False?**

An alkane will decolourise bromine water when shaken with it.
back: **False.** Alkanes are **saturated** and do not contain a C=C double bond, so they cannot undergo addition with bromine. The bromine water remains **orange/yellow** in colour.

front: Define **unsaturated compound**.
back: An **unsaturated compound** is an organic molecule that contains at least one **C=C double bond**. It can be identified by its ability to decolourise bromine water.

front: When ethene is shaken with bromine water, an addition reaction produces **..........**,  causing the bromine water to change from **..........**  to colourless.
back: When ethene is shaken with bromine water, an addition reaction produces **1,2-dibromoethane**, causing the bromine water to change from **orange/yellow** to colourless.

front: Why does bromine water decolourise when added to an alkene?
back: Bromine undergoes an **electrophilic addition** reaction across the C=C double bond of the alkene, consuming the Br<sub>2</sub> molecules. Since the coloured Br<sub>2</sub> is used up, the solution becomes **colourless**.

front:
**True or False?**

Bromine water is orange or yellow before it reacts with an unsaturated compound.
back: **True.** Br<sub>2</sub> (aq) is **orange or yellow** in colour. Decolourisation to a colourless solution is the positive result for the test for unsaturation.

front: The test for unsaturation involves shaking the unknown compound with **..........**. A positive result is the **..........**  of the solution.
back: The test for unsaturation involves shaking the unknown compound with **bromine water**. A positive result is the **decolourisation** of the solution.

front: Define **bromine water**.
back: **Bromine water** is an aqueous solution of Br<sub>2</sub> that is orange or yellow in colour. It is used to test for **unsaturation** — decolourisation indicates the presence of a C=C double bond.

front: What type of reaction occurs between an alkene and bromine water, and what product is formed from ethene?
back: An **electrophilic addition** reaction occurs. Bromine adds across the C=C double bond of ethene to form **1,2-dibromoethane** (a dihalide).

front: Why are alkenes susceptible to attack by electrophiles?
back: The C=C double bond is an area of **high electron density** (four electrons). This attracts **electrophiles** (electron-loving species) that seek regions of electron density.

front:
**True or False?**

In the electrophilic addition of HBr to an alkene, the Br atom acts as the electrophile.
back: **False.** The **H** atom acts as the electrophile because it carries the partial positive charge (δ<sup>+</sup>). The H–Br bond breaks **heterolytically**, releasing Br<sup>-</sup>.

front: Define **carbocation**.
back: A **carbocation** is a highly reactive intermediate formed during electrophilic addition when a carbon atom loses a bonding electron pair and carries a **positive charge**. It is quickly attacked by a nucleophile.

front: In the electrophilic addition of HBr to ethene, the H–Br bond breaks **..........**,  forming a carbocation intermediate and a **..........**  ion.
back: In the electrophilic addition of HBr to ethene, the H–Br bond breaks **heterolytically**, forming a carbocation intermediate and a **Br**<sup>**-**</sup> ion.

front: Why does Br<sub>2</sub> act as an electrophile when it approaches an alkene, even though it is nonpolar?
back: The high electron density of the C=C double bond **repels** the electron pair in the Br–Br bond towards the far Br atom. This creates an **induced dipole** with the near Br atom becoming δ<sup>+</sup> and acting as an electrophile.

front:
**True or False?**

The addition of Br<sub>2</sub> to ethene produces a dibromoethane via a carbocation intermediate.
back: **True.** The near Br<sup>δ+</sup> accepts electrons from the C=C bond, forming a **carbocation** intermediate. The Br<sup>-</sup> ion then attacks the carbocation to give **1,2-dibromoethane**.

front: In HBr, the **..........**  atom is δ<sup>+</sup> and the **..........**  atom is δ<sup>-</sup> due to differences in electronegativity.
back: In HBr, the **H** atom is δ<sup>+</sup> and the **Br** atom is δ<sup>-</sup> due to differences in electronegativity.

front: Define **heterolytic fission**.
back: **Heterolytic fission** is the breaking of a covalent bond in which **both electrons** go to one atom, producing a cation and an anion. It occurs in electrophilic addition when the H–Br or Br–Br bond breaks.

front: What is the product of the electrophilic addition of HBr to ethene, and what is the intermediate?
back: The product is **bromoethane** (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br). The intermediate is a **primary carbocation** (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>), which is then attacked by the Br<sup>-</sup> ion.

front: Define **Markovnikov's rule**.
back: **Markovnikov's rule** is the rule that in electrophilic addition of a hydrogen halide (HX) to an alkene, the halogen bonds to the **most substituted** carbon atom, forming the **major** product via the most stable carbocation intermediate.

front: Why is a tertiary carbocation more stable than a primary carbocation?
back: A tertiary carbocation has **three alkyl groups** attached to the positively charged carbon. Each alkyl group donates electron density towards the cation through the **inductive effect**, spreading the positive charge and making the ion more stable.

front:
**True or False?**

In the electrophilic addition of HBr to propene, the major product is 1-bromopropane.
back: **False.** The major product is **2-bromopropane**. The H<sup>+</sup> attaches to the least substituted carbon, giving the more stable **secondary carbocation**, which then reacts with Br<sup>-</sup> to give 2-bromopropane.

front: The stability order of carbocations is: **..........**  > secondary > **..........**,  because more alkyl groups donate greater electron density via the inductive effect.
back: The stability order of carbocations is: **tertiary** > secondary > **primary**, because more alkyl groups donate greater electron density via the inductive effect.

front: What is the inductive effect in the context of carbocation stability?
back: The **inductive effect** is the donation of electron density from **alkyl groups** towards the positively charged carbon of a carbocation. This reduces the positive charge and distributes it over more atoms, making the carbocation more **energetically stable**.

front:
**True or False?**

Carbocations are nucleophiles because they carry a positive charge.
back: **False.** Carbocations are **electrophiles** — they are electron-deficient species attracted to regions of high electron density. Nucleophiles carry negative charge or lone pairs.

front: Markovnikov's rule predicts that when HBr adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the H<sup>+</sup> adds to the **..........**  carbon, and the Br<sup>-</sup> adds to the **..........**  carbon.
back: Markovnikov's rule predicts that when HBr adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the H<sup>+</sup> adds to the **least substituted** carbon, and the Br<sup>-</sup> adds to the **most substituted** carbon.

front: Define **anti-Markovnikov addition**.
back: **Anti-Markovnikov addition** is the minor pathway in electrophilic addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene, in which the halogen bonds to the **least substituted** carbon via the less stable carbocation intermediate.

front: In the reaction of propene with HBr, what are the two carbocation intermediates and which gives the major product?
back: The two intermediates are a **secondary carbocation** (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sup>+</sup>CH<sub>3</sub>) and a **primary carbocation** (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>). The secondary carbocation is more stable and gives the **major product**, 2-bromopropane.

front: Define **halogenoalkane**.
back: A **halogenoalkane** is an alkane in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by a **halogen** atom. They are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary based on the substitution of the carbon bearing the halogen.

front: Name three routes by which halogenoalkanes can be produced.
back:
1. **Free-radical substitution** of alkanes with Cl<sub>2</sub> or Br<sub>2</sub> in UV light.
2. **Electrophilic addition** of HX or X<sub>2</sub> to alkenes.
3. **Substitution** of an alcohol using HX, PCl<sub>3</sub>, PCl<sub>5</sub> or SOCl<sub>2</sub>.

front:
**True or False?**

A secondary halogenoalkane has the halogen bonded to a carbon that is attached to three other alkyl groups.
back: **False.** A **secondary** halogenoalkane has the halogen on a carbon attached to **two** alkyl groups. Three alkyl groups defines a **tertiary** halogenoalkane.

front: When an alcohol reacts with PCl<sub>5</sub> at room temperature, the –OH group is replaced by **..........**,  producing a **..........**  and HCl.
back: When an alcohol reacts with PCl<sub>5</sub> at room temperature, the –OH group is replaced by **–Cl**, producing a **chloroalkane** and HCl.

front: What is the major product rule when HBr adds to an unsymmetrical alkene to form a halogenoalkane?
back: The major product has Br bonded to the **most substituted** carbon (**Markovnikov's rule**). This is because the more substituted carbon gives the more stable **carbocation** intermediate.

front:
**True or False?**

Electrophilic addition of a halogen (X<sub>2</sub>) to an alkene proceeds with one halogen atom acting as an electrophile and the other as a nucleophile.
back: **True.** When X<sub>2</sub> approaches the electron-rich C=C bond, one X atom becomes δ<sup>+</sup> (the **electrophile**) and the other becomes X<sup>-</sup> (the **nucleophile**) after the X–X bond breaks heterolytically.

front: A **..........**  halogenoalkane has the halogen on a carbon bonded to one alkyl group. A **..........**  halogenoalkane has it bonded to two alkyl groups.
back: A **primary** halogenoalkane has the halogen on a carbon bonded to one alkyl group. A **secondary** halogenoalkane has it bonded to two alkyl groups.

front: Define **tertiary halogenoalkane**.
back: A **tertiary halogenoalkane** is one in which the halogen is bonded to a carbon atom that is itself attached to **three** other alkyl groups.

front: What reagent and conditions convert an alcohol to a chloroalkane using thionyl chloride?
back: The alcohol is reacted with **SOCl**<sub>**2**</sub> (thionyl chloride). The reaction replaces the –OH group with –Cl to form the **chloroalkane**, releasing SO<sub>2</sub> and HCl as by-products.

front: Define **nucleophilic substitution**.
back: **Nucleophilic substitution** is a reaction in which a **nucleophile** attacks a carbon atom carrying a δ<sup>+</sup> charge, replacing the atom or group carrying a δ<sup>-</sup> charge (the **leaving group**).

front: What product is formed when a halogenoalkane reacts with ethanolic KCN under reflux, and why is this reaction useful?
back: A **nitrile** is formed (e.g. bromoethane + KCN → propanenitrile). The reaction is useful because it adds one **extra carbon atom** to the chain, extending the carbon skeleton of the starting material.

front:
**True or False?**

The hydroxide ion is a better nucleophile than water because it carries a full formal negative charge.
back: **True.** OH<sup>-</sup> has a **full negative charge**, making it a stronger nucleophile than water, where the oxygen only has a **partial negative charge** (δ<sup>-</sup>). Nucleophilic substitution with OH<sup>-</sup> is therefore much faster than with water.

front: When bromoethane reacts with excess ethanolic **..........** under pressure, the primary product is **..........** (an amine).
back: When bromoethane reacts with excess ethanolic **ammonia (NH**<sub>**3**</sub>**)** under pressure, the primary product is **ethylamine (CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**NH**<sub>**2**</sub>**)** (an amine).

front: Why must ammonia be used in excess in the nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane?
back: The primary amine product (e.g. ethylamine) can itself act as a **nucleophile** and attack another halogenoalkane molecule, forming a **secondary amine** (e.g. diethylamine). Excess NH<sub>3</sub> minimises this over-substitution.

front:
**True or False?**

Iodoalkanes hydrolyse faster than bromoalkanes in aqueous silver nitrate because the C–I bond is shorter and stronger.
back: **False.** Iodoalkanes hydrolyse **faster** because the C–I bond is the **weakest and longest** of the C–halogen bonds, making it easier to break in nucleophilic substitution.

front: In the reaction of a halogenoalkane with aqueous NaOH, the nucleophile is **..........**  and the product is a/an **..........**.
back: In the reaction of a halogenoalkane with aqueous NaOH, the nucleophile is **OH**<sup>**-**</sup> and the product is an **alcohol**.

front: Define **hydrolysis**.
back: **Hydrolysis** is the breakdown of a molecule by **water**. In the context of halogenoalkanes, it refers to nucleophilic substitution by water (or OH<sup>-</sup>) to produce an **alcohol** and a halide ion.

front: How can aqueous silver nitrate be used to identify which halogen is present in a halogenoalkane?
back: Water in the AgNO<sub>3</sub> solution **hydrolyses** the halogenoalkane, releasing halide ions. These react with Ag<sup>+</sup> to form **coloured precipitates**: AgCl (white), AgBr (cream) or AgI (yellow). The rate of precipitate formation also indicates bond strength.

front: What reagent and conditions are required for the elimination reaction of a halogenoalkane?
back: The halogenoalkane is heated with **ethanolic sodium hydroxide** (NaOH dissolved in ethanol). The anhydrous conditions favour **elimination** to produce an alkene.

front:
**True or False?**

Heating a halogenoalkane with aqueous NaOH produces an alkene by elimination.
back: **False.** Aqueous NaOH favours **nucleophilic substitution**, producing an **alcohol**. Ethanolic NaOH (anhydrous) is needed for the elimination reaction that produces an alkene.

front: Define **elimination reaction**.
back: An **elimination reaction** is one in which a small molecule is lost from a larger organic molecule. In halogenoalkanes, **HX** is eliminated and a **C=C double bond** forms, giving an alkene.

front: In the elimination of bromoethane, a **..........**  atom and a **..........**  atom are lost, and a C=C double bond forms to produce ethene.
back: In the elimination of bromoethane, a **hydrogen** atom and a **bromine** atom are lost, and a C=C double bond forms to produce ethene.

front: What bonds are broken and formed during the elimination of bromoethane with ethanolic NaOH?
back: The **C–Br bond** breaks heterolytically, releasing Br<sup>-</sup>. A **C–H bond** on the adjacent carbon also breaks. The electrons form a **C=C double bond**, giving ethene.

front:
**True or False?**

The small molecule eliminated from a halogenoalkane in an elimination reaction is always water.
back: **False.** In elimination reactions of halogenoalkanes, the small molecule lost is a **hydrogen halide** (e.g. HBr or HCl), not water. Water is lost in the dehydration of alcohols.

front: The overall equation for elimination of bromoethane is: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br + NaOH (ethanol) → **..........**  + NaBr + **..........** .
back: The overall equation for elimination of bromoethane is: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br + NaOH (ethanol) → **C**<sub>**2**</sub>**H**<sub>**4**</sub> + NaBr + **H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**.

front: Define **ethanolic sodium hydroxide**.
back: **Ethanolic sodium hydroxide** is NaOH dissolved in ethanol. It provides anhydrous conditions that favour **elimination** of HX from a halogenoalkane to give an **alkene**, rather than substitution.

front: State the key difference in conditions that determines whether elimination or substitution occurs when NaOH reacts with a halogenoalkane.
back: **Elimination** uses **hot ethanolic** NaOH (anhydrous, NaOH in ethanol) and produces an alkene. **Substitution** uses **warm aqueous** NaOH and produces an alcohol.

front: Define **S****<sub>N</sub>****2 mechanism**.
back: An **S**<sub>**N**</sub>**2 mechanism** is a **one-step** nucleophilic substitution in which the nucleophile attacks the δ<sup>+</sup> carbon at the same time as the C–X bond breaks. The rate depends on the concentration of **both** the halogenoalkane and the nucleophile.

front: Which type of halogenoalkane undergoes S<sub>N</sub>1 reactions, and why?
back: **Tertiary** halogenoalkanes undergo S<sub>N</sub>1 reactions because the three alkyl groups stabilise the **tertiary carbocation** intermediate through the **inductive effect**, making the C–X bond easier to break in the slow rate-determining step.

front:
**True or False?**

In an S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction, the rate-determining step is the attack of the nucleophile on the carbocation.
back: **False.** The rate-determining step in S<sub>N</sub>1 is the **slow heterolytic fission** of the C–X bond to form the **carbocation**. The nucleophile attack in the second step is fast.

front: In an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction, the nucleophile attacks at the same time as the **..........**  bond breaks. This gives a **..........**-step mechanism.
back: In an S<sub>N</sub>2 reaction, the nucleophile attacks at the same time as the **C–X** bond breaks. This gives a **one**-step mechanism.

front: What is the rate-determining step in an S<sub>N</sub>1 reaction, and what intermediate does it produce?
back: The rate-determining step is the **heterolytic fission** of the C–X bond. This is the slow first step and produces a **tertiary carbocation**. The nucleophile then attacks the carbocation in the fast second step.

front:
**True or False?**

Secondary halogenoalkanes can undergo both S<sub>N</sub>1 and S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanisms.
back: **True.** Secondary halogenoalkanes undergo a **mixture** of S<sub>N</sub>1 and S<sub>N</sub>2 reactions, depending on their specific structure and reaction conditions.

front: In S<sub>N</sub>1, the '1' means the rate depends on the concentration of the **..........**  only. In S<sub>N</sub>2, the '2' means the rate depends on the concentrations of both the halogenoalkane and the **..........**.
back: In S<sub>N</sub>1, the '1' means the rate depends on the concentration of the **halogenoalkane** only. In S<sub>N</sub>2, the '2' means the rate depends on the concentrations of both the halogenoalkane and the **nucleophile**.

front: Define **S****<sub>N</sub>****1 mechanism**.
back: An **S**<sub>**N**</sub>**1 mechanism** is a **two-step** nucleophilic substitution. In step 1 (slow, rate-determining), the C–X bond breaks to give a **carbocation**. In step 2 (fast), the nucleophile attacks the carbocation.

front: Why does a primary halogenoalkane not form a primary carbocation as an intermediate in nucleophilic substitution?
back: A **primary carbocation** is much less stable than a tertiary carbocation because it has only **one alkyl group** donating electron density via the inductive effect. Primary halogenoalkanes therefore follow the S<sub>N</sub>2 pathway, avoiding the unstable primary carbocation.

front: Why do iodoalkanes react faster in nucleophilic substitution reactions than fluoroalkanes?
back: The C–I bond has a **lower bond energy** (228 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) than the C–F bond (467 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>), so it requires less energy to break. The weaker C–I bond is therefore more easily broken during nucleophilic substitution.

front:
**True or False?**

The C–F bond is the weakest carbon-halogen bond.
back: **False.** The C–F bond is the **strongest** carbon-halogen bond (467 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>). The C–I bond is the **weakest** (228 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>), making iodoalkanes the most reactive.

front: Define **bond energy**.
back: **Bond energy** is the energy required to break one mole of a covalent bond. In halogenoalkanes, the **C–X bond energy** determines reactivity: a lower bond energy means a weaker bond and faster **nucleophilic substitution**.

front: The C–I bond energy is **..........** kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>, and the C–Cl bond energy is **..........** kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. The weaker bond leads to faster substitution.
back: The C–I bond energy is **228** kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>, and the C–Cl bond energy is **346** kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. The weaker bond leads to faster substitution.

front: What precipitates are formed when chloro-, bromo- and iodoalkanes are hydrolysed with aqueous silver nitrate, and what colours are they?
back:
1. Chloroalkane → **AgCl** (**white** precipitate).
2. Bromoalkane → **AgBr** (**cream** precipitate).
3. Iodoalkane → **AgI** (**yellow** precipitate).

front:
**True or False?**

The order of reactivity of halogenoalkanes in nucleophilic substitution is: fluoroalkanes > chloroalkanes > bromoalkanes > iodoalkanes.
back: **False.** The order is **iodoalkanes > bromoalkanes > chloroalkanes > fluoroalkanes**. Reactivity increases down Group 17 because the C–X bond becomes weaker and easier to break.

front: In aqueous AgNO<sub>3</sub>, iodoalkanes form a **..........** precipitate (AgI) most **..........** because C–I is the weakest C–X bond.
back: In aqueous AgNO<sub>3</sub>, iodoalkanes form a **yellow** precipitate (AgI) most **rapidly** because C–I is the weakest C–X bond.

front: Define **aqueous silver nitrate test**.
back: An **aqueous silver nitrate test** is a method that identifies the halogen in a halogenoalkane by hydrolysing it and observing the colour of the silver halide **precipitate** formed: AgCl (white), AgBr (cream) or AgI (yellow). The rate of formation also indicates reactivity.

front: Why is bond energy, rather than bond polarity, used to explain the reactivity trend in halogenoalkanes?
back: Although C–F is the most polar bond, **bond energy** governs reactivity here. The C–F bond is so **strong** (467 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>) that it resists heterolytic fission, making fluoroalkanes unreactive despite their polarity.

front: Define **alcohol**.
back: An **alcohol** is a compound containing at least one hydroxy (-OH) functional group, with general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+1</sub>OH.

front: What reagents and conditions are needed to produce an alcohol by electrophilic addition of an alkene?
back: **Steam** is reacted with an alkene using concentrated **phosphoric(V) acid (H**<sub>**3**</sub>**PO**<sub>**4**</sub>**)** as a catalyst and heat.

front:
**True or False?**

Cold, dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidises an alkene to form a diol without fully breaking the C=C bond.
back:
**True.**

Cold, dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub> is a mild oxidising agent. It oxidises the alkene so that both carbons of the double bond gain an -OH group, forming a diol.

front: Halogenoalkanes can be converted to alcohols by heating with **..........** . This is a **..........** substitution reaction.
back: Halogenoalkanes can be converted to alcohols by heating with **aqueous NaOH**. This is a **nucleophilic** substitution reaction.

front: What type of alcohol is formed when an aldehyde is reduced, and what reducing agents can be used?
back: Aldehydes are reduced to **primary alcohols**. Suitable reducing agents are NaBH<sub>4</sub> or LiAlH<sub>4</sub>.

front:
**True or False?**

NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol.
back:
**False.**

NaBH<sub>4</sub> is not strong enough to reduce carboxylic acids. LiAlH<sub>4</sub> must be used instead.

front: Hydrolysis of an ester with dilute acid or alkali and heat reforms a **..........** and an **..........** .
back: Hydrolysis of an ester with dilute acid or alkali and heat reforms a **carboxylic acid** and an **alcohol**.

front: What is a **diol**?
back: A **diol** is a compound containing two hydroxy (-OH) groups, formed when an alkene is oxidised by cold, dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub>.

front: Which reaction type converts a ketone into a secondary alcohol, and which reducing agents are used?
back: Reduction converts a ketone into a **secondary alcohol**. Both NaBH<sub>4</sub> and LiAlH<sub>4</sub> can be used as reducing agents.

front: Define **esterification**.
back: An **esterification** is a condensation reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, producing an ester and water, using a strong acid catalyst such as H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.

front: What products are formed when ethanol undergoes complete combustion?
back:
Complete combustion of ethanol produces **carbon dioxide** and **water**.

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O

front:
**True or False?**

Tertiary alcohols are oxidised to ketones when treated with acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>.
back:
**False.**

Tertiary alcohols do not undergo oxidation with acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>. Only primary and secondary alcohols can be oxidised.

front: When a primary alcohol is oxidised and the product is distilled off immediately, a **..........** is formed. If refluxed with excess oxidising agent, a **..........** is formed instead.
back: When a primary alcohol is oxidised and the product is distilled off immediately, an **aldehyde** is formed. If refluxed with excess oxidising agent, a **carboxylic acid** is formed instead.

front: What colour change is observed when an alcohol is oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
back: The solution changes from **orange** to **green**. The orange Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> ions are reduced to green Cr<sup>3+</sup> ions.

front:
**True or False?**

Dehydration of an alcohol is a type of elimination reaction that produces an alkene.
back:
**True.**

Dehydration removes a water molecule from the alcohol. It is an elimination reaction, producing an alkene. A hot catalyst such as Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is used.

front: Define **alkoxide**.
back: An **alkoxide** is the basic salt formed when an alcohol reacts with a reactive metal such as sodium, with hydrogen gas also produced.

front: Alcohols can be converted to halogenoalkanes by reaction with **..........**,  PCl<sub>3</sub>, PCl<sub>5</sub> or SOCl<sub>2</sub> in a **..........** substitution reaction.
back: Alcohols can be converted to halogenoalkanes by reaction with **HX**, PCl<sub>3</sub>, PCl<sub>5</sub> or SOCl<sub>2</sub> in a **substitution** reaction.

front: What product is formed when a secondary alcohol is oxidised, and does it require immediate distillation?
back: A secondary alcohol is oxidised to a **ketone**. Ketones cannot be further oxidised, so immediate distillation is not required.

front: Define **primary alcohol**.
back: A **primary alcohol** is an alcohol in which the carbon atom bonded to the -OH group is attached to one other carbon atom (or alkyl group).

front: How can acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> be used to distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols?
back: **Primary** and **secondary** alcohols both turn the orange solution **green** (they are oxidised). **Tertiary** alcohols give no colour change as they cannot be oxidised.

front:
**True or False?**

A tertiary alcohol has its -OH group attached to a carbon bonded to three other carbon atoms.
back:
**True.**

In a tertiary alcohol the carbon bearing the -OH group is bonded to three other carbon (alkyl) groups.

front: The iodoform test uses iodine in **..........**  solution. A positive result gives a yellow precipitate of **..........**.
back: The iodoform test uses iodine in **alkaline** solution. A positive result gives a yellow precipitate of **CHI**<sub>**3**</sub>.

front: Which two classes of compound give a positive iodoform test, and what structural feature do they share?
back: **Methyl ketones** (compounds with a CH<sub>3</sub>CO- group) and **ethanal** both give a positive iodoform test. They both contain the CH<sub>3</sub>CO- group.

front:
**True or False?**

Butan-2-ol gives a positive iodoform test because it can be oxidised to a methyl ketone.
back:
**True.**

Butan-2-ol has the structure CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)R, so alkaline iodine first oxidises it to butanone (a methyl ketone), which then undergoes halogenation and hydrolysis to give a yellow CHI<sub>3</sub> precipitate.

front: Define **secondary alcohol**.
back: A **secondary alcohol** is an alcohol in which the carbon atom bonded to the -OH group is attached to two other carbon atoms (or alkyl groups).

front: In the iodoform reaction, the **..........**  step replaces all three H atoms of the -CH<sub>3</sub> group with iodine. The **..........**  step then forms CHI<sub>3</sub> and a sodium carboxylate salt.
back: In the iodoform reaction, the **halogenation** step replaces all three H atoms of the -CH<sub>3</sub> group with iodine. The **hydrolysis** step then forms CHI<sub>3</sub> and a sodium carboxylate salt.

front: Why does a tertiary alcohol not change the colour of acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>?
back: A **tertiary alcohol** cannot be oxidised because the carbon bearing the -OH group has **no hydrogen atom** attached to it. Without a C-H bond at that carbon, oxidation cannot occur, so the orange colour of Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> is **unchanged**.

front: Define **positive inductive effect**.
back: A **positive inductive effect** is the donation of electron density into a covalent bond by an electron-donating group such as an alkyl group.

front: Are alcohols stronger or weaker acids than water? Give a reason.
back: Alcohols are **weaker** acids than water. The alkyl group in the alkoxide ion donates electron density to the oxygen, making it more likely to re-accept a proton and reform the alcohol, so [H<sup>+</sup>(aq)] is lower than in water.

front:
**True or False?**

Alcohols dissociate to a greater extent than water when dissolved in solution.
back:
**False.**

Alcohols have a low degree of dissociation. The equilibrium ROH ⇌ RO<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> lies far to the left, giving a lower [H<sup>+</sup>] than water.

front: In the dissociation equilibrium ROH ⇌ RO<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup>, the position of equilibrium lies to the **..........**,  meaning there are far more **..........** molecules than ions.
back: In the dissociation equilibrium ROH ⇌ RO<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup>, the position of equilibrium lies to the **left**, meaning there are far more **alcohol** molecules than ions.

front: Why does the alkoxide ion (RO<sup>-</sup>) tend to re-accept a proton more readily than the hydroxide ion (OH<sup>-</sup>)?
back: The alkoxide ion has an **electron-donating alkyl group** attached to the oxygen. This increases **electron density** on the O<sup>-</sup> atom, making it more likely to attract and accept a proton. The hydroxide ion has no such alkyl group, so its oxygen is less electron-rich.

front:
**True or False?**

The longer the hydrocarbon chain in an alcohol, the stronger the positive inductive effect and the weaker the acid.
back:
**True.**

Longer alkyl chains have a greater positive inductive effect, donating more electron density to the O<sup>-</sup> atom of the alkoxide ion, increasing its tendency to re-accept a proton and reducing the acidity further.

front: Define **alkoxide ion**.
back: An **alkoxide ion** is the negatively charged ion (RO<sup>-</sup>) formed when an alcohol loses a proton from its -OH group.

front: Alcohols are **..........**  acids because the alkyl group in the alkoxide ion has a **..........**  inductive effect, making the O<sup>-</sup> more likely to re-accept a proton.
back: Alcohols are **weaker** acids because the alkyl group in the alkoxide ion has a **positive** inductive effect, making the O<sup>-</sup> more likely to re-accept a proton.

front: What happens to the position of the equilibrium when water dissociates compared to when an alcohol dissociates?
back: In both cases the equilibrium lies to the left, but water **dissociates to a greater extent** than alcohols. Water therefore produces a **higher [H**<sup>**+**</sup>**(aq)]**, making it a **stronger acid** than alcohols.

front: Define **aldehyde**.
back: An **aldehyde** is a carbonyl compound in which the C=O group is at the end of the carbon chain, formed by oxidising a primary alcohol.

front: What colour change occurs when acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidises an alcohol?
back: The solution changes from **purple** to **colourless**. The MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> ions are reduced to colourless Mn<sup>2+</sup> ions.

front:
**True or False?**

To produce an aldehyde, the product must be distilled off as it forms to prevent further oxidation to a carboxylic acid.
back:
**True.**

Aldehydes have a lower boiling point than the alcohol they came from. Distilling the aldehyde off immediately prevents it from being further oxidised to a carboxylic acid under reflux.

front: Ketones are produced by oxidising **..........**  alcohols. Unlike aldehydes, they **..........**  undergo further oxidation.
back: Ketones are produced by oxidising **secondary** alcohols. Unlike aldehydes, they **cannot** undergo further oxidation.

front: What are the two common oxidising agents used to prepare aldehydes and ketones from alcohols?
back: **Acidified potassium dichromate(VI)** (K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) and **acidified potassium manganate(VII)** (KMnO<sub>4</sub>), both acidified with dilute sulfuric acid.

front:
**True or False?**

When K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> oxidises a secondary alcohol, the dichromate ions change from orange to green.
back:
**True.**

The orange Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> ions are reduced to green Cr<sup>3+</sup> ions as they oxidise the alcohol.

front: Define **ketone**.
back: A **ketone** is a carbonyl compound in which the C=O group is within the carbon chain (not at the end), formed by oxidising a secondary alcohol.

front: To synthesise an aldehyde, warm primary alcohol is slowly added to the **..........**  and the aldehyde is **..........**  off immediately.
back: To synthesise an aldehyde, warm primary alcohol is slowly added to the **oxidising agent** and the aldehyde is **distilled** off immediately.

front: Why does a ketone not need to be distilled off immediately after it forms during oxidation of a secondary alcohol?
back: Ketones **cannot be further oxidised**, so there is no risk of the product being converted to another compound. **Immediate distillation** is therefore unnecessary.

front: Define **hydroxynitrile**.
back: A **hydroxynitrile** is a compound containing both a hydroxy (-OH) group and a nitrile (-CN) group, formed by nucleophilic addition of HCN to an aldehyde or ketone.

front: What type of alcohol is formed when an aldehyde is reduced, and what type when a ketone is reduced?
back: Aldehydes are reduced to **primary alcohols** and ketones are reduced to **secondary alcohols**. Both NaBH<sub>4</sub> and LiAlH<sub>4</sub> can act as reducing agents.

front:
**True or False?**

In the nucleophilic addition of HCN to a carbonyl compound, the CN<sup>-</sup> ion acts as the nucleophile and attacks the carbonyl carbon.
back:
**True.**

The cyanide ion (CN<sup>-</sup>) has a lone pair on its carbon atom and attacks the slightly positive carbonyl carbon, forming a negatively charged intermediate that is then protonated to give the hydroxynitrile.

front: Aldehydes and ketones react with HCN using **..........** as a catalyst to produce **..........** .
back: Aldehydes and ketones react with HCN using **KCN** as a catalyst to produce **hydroxynitriles**.

front: What effect does nucleophilic addition of HCN have on the length of the carbon chain of an aldehyde or ketone?
back: The carbon chain **increases by one carbon atom**, as the CN<sup>-</sup> ion adds a carbon to the carbonyl compound.

front:
**True or False?**

NaBH<sub>4</sub> and LiAlH<sub>4</sub> are both suitable reducing agents for converting aldehydes and ketones to alcohols.
back:
**True.**

Both NaBH<sub>4</sub> and LiAlH<sub>4</sub> can reduce aldehydes and ketones to alcohols. NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a milder reducing agent than LiAlH<sub>4</sub>.

front: The nucleophilic addition of HCN to an aldehyde always produces a **..........** hydroxynitrile compound because a new **..........** centre is created.
back: The nucleophilic addition of HCN to an aldehyde always produces a **chiral** hydroxynitrile compound because a new **chiral** centre is created.

front: Define **nucleophilic addition**.
back: A **nucleophilic addition** is a reaction in which a nucleophile attacks and adds across a polar C=O double bond, forming a new single bond and breaking the pi bond.

front: What is the role of the cyanide ion in the nucleophilic addition of HCN to ethanal, and where does the negative charge reside on CN<sup>-</sup>?
back: CN<sup>-</sup> acts as a **nucleophile**, donating its lone pair to the carbonyl carbon. The negative charge on the cyanide ion resides on the **carbon atom**, not the nitrogen atom.

front: Define **carbonyl group**.
back: A **carbonyl group** is a C=O double bond found in aldehydes and ketones. It is polarised because oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, leaving the carbon slightly positively charged.

front: Why is the carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde or ketone susceptible to nucleophilic attack?
back: The oxygen atom is more **electronegative** than carbon, drawing **electron density** towards itself. This leaves the carbonyl carbon with a slight **positive charge (δ+)**, making it susceptible to attack by a **nucleophile**.

front:
**True or False?**

The negative charge on the cyanide ion (CN<sup>-</sup>) is located on the nitrogen atom.
back:
**False.**

The negative charge on CN<sup>-</sup> is on the **carbon atom**, not the nitrogen atom. It is the carbon end that acts as the nucleophile and attacks the carbonyl carbon.

front: In step 1 of the HCN addition mechanism, the **..........**  ion attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a **..........**  charged intermediate.
back: In step 1 of the HCN addition mechanism, the **cyanide** ion attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a **negatively** charged intermediate.

front: What happens in step 2 of the nucleophilic addition of HCN to an aldehyde?
back: The negatively charged oxygen in the intermediate reacts with an aqueous H<sup>+</sup> ion (from HCN, water or dilute acid) to form the **2-hydroxynitrile** product.

front:
**True or False?**

The addition of HCN to a carbonyl compound is a two-step mechanism involving nucleophilic attack followed by protonation.
back:
**True.**

Step 1 is nucleophilic attack of CN<sup>-</sup> on the carbonyl carbon to form a negatively charged intermediate. Step 2 is protonation of the oxygen by H<sup>+</sup> to give the hydroxynitrile.

front: The carbonyl carbon is susceptible to nucleophilic attack because the oxygen draws **..........**  density towards itself, giving the carbon a slight **..........**  charge.
back: The carbonyl carbon is susceptible to nucleophilic attack because the oxygen draws **electron** density towards itself, giving the carbon a slight **positive** charge.

front: Define **2-hydroxynitrile**.
back: A **2-hydroxynitrile** is the product of nucleophilic addition of HCN to an aldehyde or ketone, containing an -OH group and a -CN group on the same carbon atom.

front: What source of H<sup>+</sup> ions can protonate the negatively charged intermediate in step 2 of the HCN addition mechanism?
back: H<sup>+</sup> ions can come from **HCN** itself, from **water** or from **dilute acid** present in solution.

front: Define **2,4-DNPH**.
back: A **2,4-DNPH** (2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine) is a reagent used to detect carbonyl compounds. It reacts with aldehydes and ketones in a condensation reaction to produce a deep-orange precipitate.

front: How can the identity of a specific aldehyde or ketone be confirmed after a positive 2,4-DNPH test?
back: The deep-orange precipitate is purified by **recrystallisation** and its **melting point** is measured. The value is compared with literature values to identify the specific carbonyl compound.

front:
**True or False?**

Carboxylic acids and esters give a positive result with 2,4-DNPH.
back:
**False.**

Only aldehydes and ketones give a positive result. Carboxylic acids and esters do not react with 2,4-DNPH to form a precipitate.

front: Tollens' reagent is an aqueous alkaline solution of **..........**  in excess **..........**  solution.
back: Tollens' reagent is an aqueous alkaline solution of **silver nitrate** in excess **ammonia** solution.

front: What observation is made when an aldehyde is warmed with Tollens' reagent, and what is reduced?
back: A **silver mirror** forms on the inside of the tube. The Ag<sup>+</sup> ions are reduced to silver atoms (Ag) as they oxidise the aldehyde to a carboxylate ion.

front:
**True or False?**

Ketones give a positive result with both Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent.
back:
**False.**

Ketones cannot be oxidised and therefore give a **negative** result with both Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent. Only aldehydes give a positive result.

front: Define **Fehling's solution**.
back: A **Fehling's solution** is an alkaline solution containing Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions used to test for aldehydes. A positive result produces a red precipitate of copper(I) oxide as the clear blue solution turns opaque.

front: When an aldehyde is warmed with Fehling's solution, the **..........**  Cu<sup>2+</sup> solution turns **..........**  due to the formation of copper(I) oxide.
back: When an aldehyde is warmed with Fehling's solution, the **clear blue** Cu<sup>2+</sup> solution turns **opaque red** due to the formation of copper(I) oxide.

front: What type of reaction occurs between 2,4-DNPH and a carbonyl compound, and what small molecule is eliminated?
back: A **condensation reaction** occurs. A **water** molecule is eliminated as the 2,4-DNPH and carbonyl compound join together to form the deep-orange precipitate.

front: Define **tri-iodomethane (iodoform)**.
back: A **tri-iodomethane** (iodoform, CHI<sub>3</sub>) is a yellow precipitate formed in the iodoform reaction when methyl ketones or ethanal are heated with iodine in alkaline solution.

front: Which structural feature must a compound have to give a positive iodoform test?
back: The compound must contain a **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CO-** group (a methyl ketone). Ethanal also contains this group and gives a positive test.

front:
**True or False?**

Ethanal gives a positive iodoform test because it contains a CH<sub>3</sub>CO- group.
back:
**True.**

Ethanal (CH<sub>3</sub>CHO) contains the CH<sub>3</sub>CO- group, so it undergoes the iodoform reaction to produce a yellow CHI<sub>3</sub> precipitate.

front: In the iodoform reaction, the reagent is heated with an **..........**  solution of iodine. The yellow precipitate formed is **..........**.
back: In the iodoform reaction, the reagent is heated with an **alkaline** solution of iodine. The yellow precipitate formed is **CHI**<sub>**3**</sub>.

front: Describe the two steps of the iodoform reaction.
back:
**Step 1 (halogenation):** All three H atoms of the -CH<sub>3</sub> group are replaced by iodine atoms to form a **-CI**<sub>**3**</sub> group.

**Step 2 (hydrolysis):** The intermediate is hydrolysed by alkaline solution to form a **sodium carboxylate salt** (RCO<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup> Na<sup>+</sup>) and the yellow **CHI**<sub>**3**</sub> precipitate.

front:
**True or False?**

Propanone gives a positive iodoform test because it is a methyl ketone.
back:
**True.**

Propanone (CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>) contains a CH<sub>3</sub>CO- group, so it undergoes the iodoform reaction with alkaline iodine to produce a yellow CHI<sub>3</sub> precipitate.

front: In the halogenation step of the iodoform reaction, **..........**  iodine atoms replace the hydrogen atoms of the **..........**  group in the methyl ketone.
back: In the halogenation step of the iodoform reaction, **three** iodine atoms replace the hydrogen atoms of the **-CH**<sub>**3**</sub> group in the methyl ketone.

front: Define **methyl ketone**.
back: A **methyl ketone** is a ketone containing a CH<sub>3</sub>CO- group, which reacts with iodine in alkaline solution to form the yellow precipitate CHI<sub>3</sub> (iodoform).

front: What are the two products formed in the hydrolysis step of the iodoform reaction?
back: The two products are a **sodium carboxylate salt** (RCO<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup> Na<sup>+</sup>) and a **yellow precipitate of CHI**<sub>**3**</sub> (tri-iodomethane / iodoform).

front: Define **carboxylic acid**.
back: A **carboxylic acid** is a compound containing the -COOH functional group. It is a weak acid that partially dissociates in water, giving a pH below 7.

front: Name three ways carboxylic acids can be produced.
back:
1. **Oxidation** of primary alcohols or aldehydes with acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> or acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> under reflux.
2. **Hydrolysis of nitriles** using dilute acid or dilute alkali followed by acidification.
3. **Hydrolysis of esters** using dilute acid or dilute alkali followed by acidification.

front:
**True or False?**

Hydrolysis of a nitrile with dilute acid forms a carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt.
back:
**True.**

Acid hydrolysis of a nitrile converts the -CN group to a -COOH group and also produces an ammonium salt.

front: Carboxylic acids are **..........**  acids because they only **..........**  dissociate in water, leaving the equilibrium position to the left.
back: Carboxylic acids are **weak** acids because they only **partially** dissociate in water, leaving the equilibrium position to the left.

front: What is observed and what gas is produced when a carboxylic acid reacts with a carbonate?
back: The carbonate **fizzes** and **carbon dioxide** gas is produced. The reaction is an acid-base reaction forming a salt and water alongside the CO<sub>2</sub>(g).

front:
**True or False?**

LiAlH<sub>4</sub> can reduce a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol, but NaBH<sub>4</sub> cannot.
back:
**True.**

LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a stronger reducing agent than NaBH<sub>4</sub> and can reduce carboxylic acids to primary alcohols. NaBH<sub>4</sub> is not powerful enough for this reaction.

front: Alkaline hydrolysis of an ester is an **..........**  reaction that first forms a sodium **..........**  salt, which requires acidification to give the carboxylic acid.
back: Alkaline hydrolysis of an ester is an **irreversible** reaction that first forms a sodium **carboxylate** salt, which requires acidification to give the carboxylic acid.

front: Define **hydrolysis**.
back: A **hydrolysis** is the breakdown of a compound using water (or dilute acid/alkali), converting functional groups such as -CN or -COOR into -COOH.

front: What type of reaction is esterification, and what are the reagents and conditions needed?
back: Esterification is a **condensation reaction** between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, heated under reflux with a strong acid catalyst (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> or H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>), producing an ester and water.

front: Define **amine**.
back: An **amine** is a compound containing the -NH<sub>2</sub> functional group, formed by nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane with ammonia.

front: What reagents and conditions are needed to produce an amine from a halogenoalkane?
back: The halogenoalkane is heated under pressure with **ethanolic ammonia** (NH<sub>3</sub> dissolved in ethanol).

front:
**True or False?**

The nitrogen atom in ammonia acts as a nucleophile because it has a lone pair of electrons.
back:
**True.**

The lone pair on the nitrogen of NH<sub>3</sub> attacks the partial positive carbon of the C-X bond in the halogenoalkane, replacing the halogen in a nucleophilic substitution reaction.

front: In the nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane by NH<sub>3</sub>, the **..........**  atom of ammonia attacks the **..........**  charged carbon of the C-X bond.
back: In the nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane by NH<sub>3</sub>, the **nitrogen** atom of ammonia attacks the **partially positive** charged carbon of the C-X bond.

front: Why does the C-X bond in a halogenoalkane have a partial positive charge on the carbon?
back: The halogen atom is more **electronegative** than carbon, so it draws electron density away from the C-X bond towards itself. This gives the carbon a partial positive charge (δ+) and the halogen a partial negative charge (δ-).

front:
**True or False?**

Reacting bromoethane with ethanolic ammonia under heat and pressure produces ethylamine and hydrobromic acid.
back:
**True.**

The NH<sub>3</sub> substitutes the Br in bromoethane via nucleophilic substitution, forming ethylamine (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) and hydrobromic acid (HBr) as the byproduct.

front: Amines are produced from halogenoalkanes by **..........**  substitution, in which the halogen is replaced by an **..........**  group.
back: Amines are produced from halogenoalkanes by **nucleophilic** substitution, in which the halogen is replaced by an **amine** group.

front: Define **nucleophile**.
back: A **nucleophile** is an electron-pair donor that attacks electron-deficient (partial positive) atoms. The nitrogen lone pair in NH<sub>3</sub> acts as a nucleophile in the production of amines.

front: Why is an ethanolic solution of ammonia used rather than an aqueous solution to produce amines from halogenoalkanes?
back: Aqueous ammonia contains water, which can act as a nucleophile and cause **hydrolysis** of the halogenoalkane, producing an **alcohol** as a competing product. Using **ethanolic ammonia** removes water, ensuring NH<sub>3</sub> is the only nucleophile present and the reaction selectively produces the **amine**.

front: Define **nitrile**.
back: A **nitrile** is a compound containing the -CN functional group, prepared by nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane with ethanolic KCN.

front: What reagents and conditions are needed to convert a halogenoalkane into a nitrile?
back: The halogenoalkane is heated under reflux with an **ethanolic solution of potassium cyanide (KCN in ethanol)**. The CN<sup>-</sup> ion acts as the nucleophile.

front:
**True or False?**

The reaction of a halogenoalkane with ethanolic KCN increases the length of the carbon chain by one carbon atom.
back:
**True.**

The CN<sup>-</sup> ion adds a carbon atom to the chain as it substitutes the halogen. This makes the reaction useful for chain extension in synthesis.
